items.title: James Gray, Luca Guadagnino, Xavier Dolan… les cinéastes à l'honneur des « Conversations » du FIFM
items.description: Au-delà des films et des tapis rouges, le Festival international du film de Marrakech entend mettre en lumière les parcours, les expériences et les réflexions de celles et ceux qui façonnent le septième art. Pour sa 23e édition, prévue du 20 au 28 novembre, le rendez-vous cinématographique reconduit son programme « Conversations », consacré aux échanges directs entre le public et des personnalités majeures du cinéma international. Au fil des éditions, ces rencontres se sont imposées comme l'un des temps forts du Festival. L'ambition est de donner à voir ce qui échappe habituellement à l'écran : les rencontres déterminantes, les intuitions, les prises de risque, les hésitations et les passions qui ont jalonné les trajectoires artistiques. Selon les organisateurs, ces échanges offrent aux cinéastes et aux comédiens un espace de parole libre, loin des discours promotionnels et des interventions convenues. Ils permettent ainsi de revenir sur les moments décisifs de leur carrière, leurs inspirations et leurs convictions, mais aussi sur les circonstances et les rencontres qui ont contribué à façonner leur parcours. Cette année, plusieurs figures emblématiques du cinéma mondial se prêteront à l'exercice. Parmi elles, Jeff Goldblum et John Turturro, auxquels le Festival rendra également hommage. Le premier reviendra sur une carrière de près de six décennies, marquée notamment par « La Mouche », « Jurassic Park » et, plus récemment, « Wicked ». Connu pour son humour, son élégance singulière et son jeu immédiatement reconnaissable, l'acteur américain partagera les différentes étapes de son parcours. John Turturro, acteur incontournable du cinéma indépendant américain, notamment associé aux frères Coen et à Spike Lee, évoquera quant à lui les multiples dimensions de sa carrière. Des productions indépendantes aux grands films hollywoodiens, en passant par ses propres réalisations, son parcours témoigne d'une relation plurielle au cinéma. Autre invitée de marque, Monica Bellucci reviendra sur une carrière internationale construite au fil de collaborations et de productions aux horizons variés. De « L'Appartement » à « Malèna », en passant par « Irréversible », « Matrix » et « 007 Spectre », l'actrice italienne a évolué entre plusieurs pays et plusieurs langues. Récemment à l'affiche de « Beetlejuice Beetlejuice », elle partagera son expérience d'un parcours qui l'a conduite à travailler avec des cinéastes aux univers particulièrement différents. Le programme fera également une place aux auteurs dont les films interrogent les liens familiaux, les trajectoires individuelles et les fractures de la société. Le réalisateur américain James Gray reviendra sur son regard porté sur l'Amérique, qu'il explore depuis « Little Odessa » jusqu'à « Armageddon Time ». Son nouveau long-métrage, « Paper Tiger », sera également présenté lors de cette édition. Son cinéma, marqué par une attention particulière aux relations familiales, aux origines et aux rêves contrariés, constitue le fil conducteur de son œuvre. Le cinéaste roumain Cristian Mungiu sera lui aussi au rendez-vous. Lauréat en mai dernier de sa deuxième Palme d'or au Festival de Cannes pour « Fjord », dix-neuf ans après avoir été récompensé pour « 4 mois, 3 semaines et 2 jours », il reviendra sur une filmographie profondément ancrée dans les réalités sociales et les dilemmes moraux contemporains. Le cinéma marocain sera représenté par la réalisatrice Laïla Marrakchi. Son premier long-métrage, « Marock », avait marqué le paysage cinématographique national en abordant sans détour les aspirations et les contradictions de la jeunesse. De ce film à « La más dulce », présenté cette année à Marrakech, en passant par ses réalisations télévisuelles, la cinéaste a développé une œuvre attentive aux rapports familiaux, aux normes sociales et à la question de la liberté individuelle, sur fond de transformations de la société marocaine. Le réalisateur italien Luca Guadagnino figure également parmi les invités. De « Call Me by Your Name » à « Challengers », son cinéma explore les thèmes du désir, de la sensualité et de la transgression. Il présentera à Marrakech son nouveau film, « Artificial », consacré aux coulisses de l'intelligence artificielle, et reviendra sur les différentes étapes de son parcours artistique. La programmation accueillera par ailleurs Xavier Dolan, révélé à l'âge de 19 ans avec « J'ai tué ma mère ». Le cinéaste canadien, qui a ensuite obtenu le Prix du jury à Cannes pour « Mommy », puis le Grand Prix pour « Juste la fin du monde », évoquera une carrière précoce et singulière. Son cinéma, profondément personnel, accorde une place centrale aux relations familiales, aux émotions et aux questions identitaires. Dans un registre différent, le réalisateur américain Rian Johnson reviendra sur son travail autour du film à énigme, dont il a contribué à renouveler les codes avec « À couteaux tirés » et sa suite, « Glass Onion : une histoire à couteaux tirés ». De « Brick » à « Looper », jusqu'à « Star Wars : Les Derniers Jedi », son parcours témoigne d'un intérêt constant pour les récits à rebondissements, les personnages imprévisibles et les constructions narratives complexes. Le cinéma français sera notamment représenté par Gilles Lellouche. L'acteur, parmi les plus populaires de sa génération, reviendra sur son parcours derrière la caméra, amorcé avec « Narco », coréalisé avec Tristan Aurouet, puis poursuivi avec « Le Grand Bain » et « L'Amour ouf », deux films présentés au Festival de Cannes. Enfin, Arthur Harari évoquera son travail de réalisateur et de scénariste. Remarqué pour « Diamant noir », « Onoda, 10.000 nuits dans la jungle » et « L'Inconnue », récompensé par le prix Jean-Vigo, il a également remporté l'Oscar du meilleur scénario original pour « Anatomie d'une chute », coécrit avec Justine Triet. Son œuvre se distingue notamment par son intérêt pour les personnages complexes et les destins hors du commun. À travers cette sélection d'artistes aux parcours et aux sensibilités contrastés, les « Conversations » entendent offrir un aperçu des différentes expressions du cinéma contemporain. Des grandes productions hollywoodiennes aux œuvres d'auteur, des films de genre aux récits intimistes, ces rencontres seront l'occasion d'explorer les multiples manières dont le cinéma raconte le monde, questionne les sociétés et entre en résonance avec les spectateurs, souligne le communiqué du Festival. The post James Gray, Luca Guadagnino, Xavier Dolan… les cinéastes à l'honneur des « Conversations » du FIFM appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Troops rescue three kidnap victims, kill two terrorists in Adamawa
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi Troops of Operation Hadin Kai (OPHK) have rescued three kidnapped civilians and killed two terrorists in separate operations in Adamawa State. The troops also recovered two AK-47 rifles, ammunition, locally fabricated explosive devices, stolen vehicles and farm produce belonging to residents who narrowly escaped abduction. The Acting Media Information Officer of OPHK, Capt. Mohammed Goni, disclosed this in a statement on Tuesday. He said the three victims were rescued by troops deployed in Mubi following a distress call from farmers around Dutse-Uku in Mubi South Local Government Area. According to him, suspected kidnappers abducted a farmer, identified as Happiness Dama Dauda, on November 9 while she was working on her farm and also stole her motorcycle. Goni said the troops, working with local hunters, mobilised to the area and mounted pressure on the kidnappers, forcing them to abandon their victim and flee. He added that a sustained pursuit led to the rescue of two other residents suspected to have been abducted earlier, bringing the number of rescued victims to three. The troops also recovered a motorcycle, a tricycle conveying 15 bags of beans and a Hi-Jet pickup carrying 13 bags of groundnuts belonging to other farmers who narrowly escaped abduction. Goni said the respective village heads identified the recovered items, which were subsequently handed over to their owners. Two terrorists killed in Gombi In a separate operation on November 8, troops deployed at Zangula Kilba Junction in Gombi Local Government Area foiled an attempted attack by suspected Boko Haram/Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) terrorists. Two terrorists were killed during the encounter, while others fled following what the military described as the troops’ superior combat readiness and tactical resilience. Items recovered from the fleeing insurgents included two AK-47 rifles, four magazines, 115 rounds of ammunition, three belts of empty ammunition links and two cases of locally fabricated explosive devices. Other recovered items included a pair of desert boots, a backpack, an Android phone, a wristwatch and N15,000. Goni said troops had commenced exploitation operations to track down the fleeing terrorists and prevent them from regrouping. He added that troops were maintaining aggressive patrols and surveillance across the affected areas to prevent further attacks and reassure residents of their safety. The military urged residents to provide timely and credible intelligence to security agencies, stressing that collaboration between troops and local communities remained critical to tackling terrorism and other security threats. Operation Hadin Kai reaffirmed its commitment to sustaining operational pressure on terrorists and their collaborators to deny them the freedom to threaten the security and livelihoods of residents across the North-East. The post Troops rescue three kidnap victims, kill two terrorists in Adamawa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Togo-Banque mondiale : un partenariat dynamique au service du développement socioéconomique
items.description: Le renforcement de la coopération entre le Togo et le Groupe de la Banque mondiale était au centre des échanges, ce lundi 9 novembre 2026, entre le Président du Conseil, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, et le Vice-président du Groupe de la Banque mondiale pour l’Afrique de l’ouest et du centre, Ousmane Diagana. Cette rencontre a permis de faire le point sur l’état du partenariat entre le Togo et l’institution financière internationale, d’apprécier les progrès accomplis et d’explorer de nouvelles perspectives de coopération, dans un contexte marqué par les enjeux de transformation économique et de développement durable. Le Vice-président du Groupe de la Banque mondiale pour l’Afrique de l’ouest et du centre s’est félicité de la qualité des relations entre les deux parties et a réaffirmé l’engagement de l’institution à accompagner les ambitions de développement du Togo. « C’est un partenariat qui se porte très bien. L’objectif cardinal est de soutenir l’économie togolaise pour créer davantage d’emplois et de meilleurs emplois, en particulier pour les jeunes et pour les femmes. Ce qui est une condition essentielle pour la prospérité partagée et la lutte contre la pauvreté, qui sont les objectifs essentiels des missions de la Banque mondiale », a-t-il précisé. Les discussions ont particulièrement porté sur les moyens de renforcer le potentiel du secteur agricole et d’en faire un véritable levier de développement économique et de création d’emplois. A cet égard, le Vice-président de la Banque mondiale pour l’Afrique de l’ouest et du centre a souligné l’importance d’une nouvelle approche de développement de l’agriculture, qui dépasse sa seule fonction de production alimentaire pour en faire également un secteur générateur d’activités économiques et d’emplois. « Nous avons échangé avec Son Excellence Monsieur le Président du Conseil sur le rôle de la Banque mondiale pour faire véritablement de l’agriculture un secteur de développement, qui non seulement assure la sécurité alimentaire au niveau du pays, mais également crée des emplois à travers une approche nouvelle où le paysan n’est pas qu’un agriculteur, il est également un entrepreneur », a-t-il expliqué. Au-delà de l’agriculture, les échanges ont également porté sur le financement des investissements dans d’autres secteurs prioritaires à fort potentiel de croissance et de création d’emplois, notamment l’énergie et l’économie numérique. Le développement du capital humain, à travers l’éducation, la formation professionnelle, la santé et la nutrition, constitue également un axe important de cette coopération. Monsieur Ousmane Diagana a également abordé avec le Président du Conseil, les défis sécuritaires et environnementaux auxquels le Togo et les autres pays de la sous-région ouest-africaine sont confrontés. Les tensions et les conflits dans certaines parties de la région, conjugués aux effets des changements climatiques, constituent autant de facteurs qui affectent les perspectives de développement et appellent des réponses concertées. Pour rappel, le Cadre de partenariat pays (CPP) 2025-2029, qui définit les grandes orientations de l’intervention du Groupe de la Banque mondiale au Togo, s’articule autour de trois axes majeurs, à savoir l’amélioration de la qualité des emplois dans le secteur privé, le renforcement du capital humain et la promotion d’un développement territorial inclusif et résilient. A travers cette coopération, le Togo entend poursuivre ses efforts de transformation économique et sociale, avec l’appui de la Banque mondiale, autour de priorités structurantes pour la croissance, l’emploi et l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations.

items.title: Dr Sylla Thiam associe science et islam
items.description: La Santé publique est un immense chantier de recherches. Pour apporter sa pièce à l’édifice, Dr Sylla Thiam a publié un livre dans lequel, il associe l’islam et la science afin de permettre de faciliter la prise en charge sanitaire des populations. Devant sa famille, ses amis et ses collègues, Dr Sylla Thiam, médecin en santé publique a présenté, le weekend dernier, à Dakar, son livre intitulé « Agir sur les déterminants de la Santé, quels enseignements tirer de l’Islam pour promouvoir la santé publique ». Médecin, chercheur et expert en santé publique, fort de plus de vingt ans d'expérience, l'auteur propose dans son livre une approche interdisciplinaire qui s’articule autour de cinq grands déterminants. Il s’agit de la génétique, de la biologie, la nutrition, le mode de vie, l'environnement et le système de santé. À travers ces déterminants, il veut montrer comment les prescriptions du Coran et de la « Sunna » peuvent contribuer à renforcer la prévention. Il a rappelé que les stratégies de santé publique ne peuvent produire pleinement leurs effets lorsqu'elles ignorent les réalités culturelles et religieuses des populations auxquelles elles s'adressent. Il souligne aussi que les stratégies sanitaires doivent être en concordance avec les croyances religieuses. L’ouvrage de 225 pages, préfacé par le Pr Masserigne Soumaré, a été présenté, lors de la cérémonie de dédicace, par Pr Lamine Gueye. Dans sa présentation, il fait savoir que, lire ce livre, revient à méditer sur l'islam et la science, car l’auteur a utilisé 206 références scientifiques modernes, 32 autres références sur les versets du Coran, 78 citations tirées aussi du Coran, et 49 hadiths de grands érudits connus dans le monde musulman comme Boukhari, Muslim. Le Pr Lamine Gueye précise que « chaque affirmation de l'auteur, déduction scientifique, recommandation Islamique est illustrée par un effort de justification, de raisonnement, d'utilisation de références faisant appel à la science moderne ou islamique ». Il estime que l’ouvrage constitue une belle contribution à la littérature sanitaire, religieuse, avec une réelle originalité. Marie Bernadette SÈNE

items.title: Madonna University: 15 nursing students beg for expulsion, suspension reversal over TikTok video
items.description: By Chioma Okoye Fifteen nursing students of Madonna University, Nigeria, have appealed to the university management to reverse their expulsion and suspension over a controversial TikTok video recorded during their community posting, pleading for another opportunity to complete their studies. The students, in a letter dated November 2, 2026, tendered an unreserved apology to the management, admitting that their conduct was unethical and had brought disrepute to the nursing profession and the university community. The video, which went viral on social media, sparked widespread reactions and prompted disciplinary action by the university management. In the appeal addressed to the university management through the Registrar, the students said they had reflected deeply on their actions and were genuinely remorseful. “We sincerely regret our said actions and assure the University Management and all relevant authorities that such an incident will not repeat itself again,” they said. They pleaded with the management to reconsider its decision, stressing that their families had made significant sacrifices to support their education and enable them to reach the present stage of their academic journey. The students said reversing the expulsion would give them an opportunity to complete their programmes and pursue their chosen professional careers instead of having their academic aspirations cut short. They also appreciated the university management for engaging with their parents and guardians and allowing them to present their concerns. According to the students, they did not take the gesture for granted and remained grateful for the opportunity given to their families to be heard. The appeal, jointly signed by the 15 students, urged the university management to reconsider the punishment and give them a second chance. See the letter below: Vanguard Newspaper The post Madonna University: 15 nursing students beg for expulsion, suspension reversal over TikTok video appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tinubu’s achievements will make it difficult to unseat him – Wike
items.description: The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Mr Nyesom Wike, says it will be immensely difficult for opposition parties to unseat President Bola Tinubu in the upcoming 2027 general elections. Wike said this in Abuja on Tuesday, after inspecting some ongoing projects within the federal capital territory. He cited what he described as Tinubu’s undeniable and rich report card of infrastructure development across the country. The minister said that the volume and pace of visible achievements delivered under Tinubu’s administration left very little room for political detractors to challenge the ruling party’s record. “You can see clearly that it will be difficult to unseat the president today because the report card is obvious in terms of what he has done. “Like I told you, this is our campaign. People ask what we are going to campaign with, but we have so many visible achievements all around us. “There is no way residents of Abuja will see the kind of infrastructure we have provided and say they are not happy with the achievements of Mr President. It is second to none,” he said. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the minister inspected the ongoing construction of Innet Southern Motorway, from the Area 1 roundabout to the Games Village bridges and Southern Parkway, linking Oladipo Diya Road with Ring Road II. He also inspected the ongoing construction of the Arterial Road S1 project in Abuja to connect Ring Road II to the FCT Fire Service Station in the Kaura and Gaduwa district corridors. Highlighting the rapid speed of execution on several key projects in the territory, Wike referenced the rapid transformation of the Southern Parkway project, which was flagged during the celebration of Tinubu’s third year in office. “Within six to seven months, you can see what has been achieved. “It is unimaginable, and that is why we are very happy,” Wike said. He pledged that the FCT administration remained on track to inaugurate at least 10 high-impact projects before the general elections scheduled for Jan. 16, 2027. (NAN) The post Tinubu’s achievements will make it difficult to unseat him – Wike appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Niamey: les ministres de l’AES engagés dans la construction d’une coopération éducative commune
items.description: La Conférence des ministres en charge de l’Éducation et de la Formation des États membres de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES) se tient du 10 au 11 novembre 2026 à Niamey, au Niger. Le camarade Jacques Sosthène DINGARA, Ministre de l’Enseignement de base, de l’Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des Langues nationales (MEBAPLN), prend part à cette rencontre qui vise à poser les bases d’un cadre permanent de concertation et de coopération entre le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger dans les domaines de l’éducation et de la formation. Le Camarade Ministre Jacques Sosthène DINGARA a été accueilli à son arrivée par son homologue nigérienne en charge de l’Enseignement de base. Cette marque d’attention traduit l’esprit de fraternité et de coopération qui anime les échanges entre les deux pays dans le domaine de l’éducation. En prélude à la conférence ministérielle, les secrétaires généraux des ministères en charge de l’Éducation et de la Formation des trois pays ont tenu une rencontre de cadrage du 6 au 9 novembre. Cette réunion préparatoire a permis d’examiner les questions inscrites à l’ordre du jour et de préparer les échanges entre les Ministres. Cette concertation traduit une volonté commune de faire de l’éducation un pilier de la souveraineté et du développement de l’espace AES. Les trois États entendent notamment renforcer leur coopération dans les domaines de l’enseignement de base, de l’alphabétisation, de la promotion des langues nationales, de l’enseignement technique et de la formation professionnelle. L’ambition est de développer des systèmes éducatifs davantage adaptés aux réalités socioculturelles des pays et aux aspirations de leurs populations. C’est dans cette dynamique que l’éducation et la formation ont été retenues parmi les domaines prioritaires du pilier « Développement » de la Confédération AES, afin d’apporter des réponses concertées aux défis communs. La feuille de route de l’An II, adoptée le 26 février 2026 à Ouagadougou, prévoit notamment la mise en place de la Conférence des ministres en charge de l’Éducation et de la Formation. Les travaux de Niamey constituent une avancée importante dans la concrétisation de cette orientation stratégique. Ils devront permettre de dégager des priorités communes, de valoriser les expériences nationales, de renforcer les complémentarités entre les systèmes éducatifs et de définir les bases d’un programme de coopération adapté aux réalités des trois pays. DCRP/MEBAPLN L’article Niamey: les ministres de l’AES engagés dans la construction d’une coopération éducative commune est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Zamfara APC crisis deepens as aspirant petitions NEC, security agencies
items.description: …Yilwatda dismisses allegations as unfounded By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — The crisis in the Zamfara State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) has taken a fresh turn, following a petition by an aspirant to the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC), National Working Committee (NWC) and security agencies over the composition of a committee to conduct a court-ordered fresh primary election. The primary is for the Kaura Namoda/Birnin Magaji Federal Constituency following an order by the Court of Appeal. The aspirant, Honourable Hassan Umar Dangaladima, accused the party’s National Chairman, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, of unilaterally constituting the committee without involving the NWC. He alleged that the committee’s composition raised concerns about its impartiality and called on the party leadership to review the arrangement before the fresh primary. In the petition, Dangaladima claimed that no NWC meeting was convened to deliberate on or approve the committee’s composition and that neither the aspirants nor the Zamfara State chapter and other relevant stakeholders were consulted. However, Yilwatda, through his Special Adviser on Media and Strategic Communication, Abimbola Tooki, dismissed the allegations as unfounded. He said the claims did not reflect the party’s established decision-making process, insisting that the NWC operated as a collective body. “The National Chairman does not operate in isolation. He works in consultation and collaboration with other members of the NWC, and decisions are taken collectively in accordance with the party’s constitution, established procedures and internal mechanisms,” Tooki said. He described the suggestion that Yilwatda single-handedly constituted the committee without the knowledge or involvement of the NWC as misleading. According to him, the APC remains committed to respecting the rule of law, implementing court directives and ensuring that its internal processes are transparent, fair and credible. “The APC is a democratic institution governed by rules and collective responsibility, not the personal preferences of any individual,” he said. Alleges committee bias Dangaladima, however, maintained that the committee’s composition raised concerns about a possible conflict of interest. He alleged that some members were loyalists, supporters or agents of another aspirant, Honourable Aminu Sani Jaji, whom he described as his main rival in the contest. The petitioner also challenged Jaji’s eligibility, alleging that his name was not contained in the APC membership register for Birnin Magaji Ward submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). He said he obtained a Certified True Copy of the register from INEC, which he attached to his petition as evidence. Dangaladima further claimed that the party had been formally notified of the alleged membership irregularity through a letter dated November 4, 2026, from his solicitors, Trinity Chambers, led by D.C. Enwelum, SAN. The letter was reportedly written in connection with Suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/1060/2026, involving Dangaladima, Jaji and other defendants. Citing Section 77(5) of the Electoral Act 2026, the aspirant argued that only party members whose names appeared in the membership register were eligible to vote or be voted for in party primaries, congresses and conventions. He consequently questioned Jaji’s eligibility to participate in the court-ordered exercise. Dangaladima also alleged that the process of selecting the committee lacked transparency, claiming that its membership was not published in advance and that aspirants were not given an opportunity to raise objections over possible conflicts of interest. He further alleged that no screening or vetting mechanism was put in place to guarantee the committee’s impartiality. According to him, the process violated the principles of natural justice, internal democracy and provisions governing the conduct of party primaries. Seeks suspension of primary The aspirant urged the APC’s NEC to suspend the fresh primary and appoint a new committee whose members would be independent and acceptable to all contestants. He warned that proceeding with the existing committee could trigger further litigation and undermine the party’s electoral prospects in Zamfara State ahead of the 2027 general elections. Copies of the petition were also sent to the APC Deputy National Chairman (North), National Vice Chairman (North-West), National Legal Adviser and Zamfara State Chairman. Others copied included the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS), the DSS Director in Zamfara State, the INEC Chairman and the Resident Electoral Commissioner for the state. Dangaladima warned that allowing the committee to conduct the primary could expose the party to further legal challenges and possible consequences for its participation in the general election. He maintained that the party was operating under a subsisting court order with a defined timeline and urged its leadership to address the issues raised before proceeding with the exercise. The post Zamfara APC crisis deepens as aspirant petitions NEC, security agencies appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: The Lost World of Aquaterra
items.description: Illustrations by Owen Pomery Imagine a planet that’s home not only to the seven continents you know but also to an immense feature you’ve never heard of, continental in scale. Extending along the world’s coastal shelves from the tropics almost to the poles, this place is roughly equivalent in size to South America, with a total area of more than 6.6 million square miles. During the last Ice Age, it consisted almost entirely of lowland ecosystems: cold grasslands and tundras in the far north, grazed by woolly mammoths and steppe bison; temperate woodlands and open country in the middle latitudes, home to aurochs, horses, and giant elk; tropical forests, grasslands, and mangrove swamps near the equator, inhabited by Stegodons, Asian hippos, and Komodo dragons; and dry scrub in the far south, roamed by marsupial lions, giant flightless birds, and lizards the size of crocodiles. Great rivers, fed by an abundance of lakes and smaller streams, cut their way through many of these lowlands, eventually opening out into marshes, lagoons, estuaries, and tidal flats as they approached the coast. Imagine that human beings settled this place after migrating out of Africa. As they dispersed, they developed technologies and vessels that allowed them to travel by sea; they devised hunting and fishing techniques that allowed them to accumulate surpluses of food and establish small permanent settlements; they buried their dead, built monumental structures, and organized themselves into social hierarchies. It may have been here, in fact—millennia before the rise of ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt—that many of the developments we associate with “civilization” first occurred. But then imagine this: Some 20,000 years ago, these lands began to flood, and by 6,000 years ago, they had disappeared entirely, taking with them much of the story of our past. As it happens, there really is such a place. You’ve almost certainly been there yourself. It has even been given a name—and, no, it’s not Atlantis. It’s Aquaterra. I first learned about Aquaterra more than a decade ago, when I received an email from the person who came up with the name—Jerome E. Dobson, a professor emeritus of geography at the University of Kansas and president emeritus of the American Geographical Society. Dobson had read a book I’d written called The Fourth Part of the World , which tells the story of a small team of Renaissance cartographers who, in 1507, became some of the first to map the giant landmass that European sailors had begun to explore across the Atlantic. To honor Amerigo Vespucci, who they believed had been the firs t to reach this “new” land, these cartographers had called the place America. [ From the January/February 2007 issue: Toby Lester on the town that gave America its name ] Dobson told me another giant “new” landmass was coming into view that deserved to be put on the map. If I wanted to learn more, he said, I should read “ Aquaterra Incognita ,” a 2014 paper he’d published in the journal Geographical Review . It’s a fascinating monograph. To understand where—and what—Aquaterra is, Dobson writes, you have to think about how sea levels fall and rise during an ice age. As the planet cools, ocean water becomes locked up in continental ice sheets, and sea levels fall by hundreds of feet. Eventually the planet starts warming again, the ice melts, and sea levels rise once more. During the past million years or so, this cycle has repeated itself many times. Today we’re living through an “interglacial,” a relatively brief warm period during which the ice sheets have retreated and sea levels are unusually high. If you were able to speed up the glacial cycle and watch it from space, you’d observe the ebb and flow of a planetary tide—one that over the course of millennia alternately exposes and submerges immense expanses of land along the continental shelves. The result, as Dobson writes, is “a vast earth feature,” bounded by the highest and lowest sea levels of the glacial cycle, that “transforms back and forth among upland, wetland, and seafloor.” This Earth feature is what he calls Aquaterra. For much of the most recent glacial cycle, Aquaterra was mainly terra, but today it’s mostly aqua. If you’ve swum or boated near almost any coastline, you’ve been there. Aquaterra isn’t just the land now underwater; it’s the whole zone that the glacial cycles have alternately drowned and exposed. That includes many of today’s beaches and coastal lowlands, which were underwater during warmer periods in the past and, as we’re now learning the hard way, are flooding again as global temperatures rise. The present-day seafloor of Aquaterra, Dobson argues, is the “least-known zone on earth”—less mapped than the floor of the deep ocean (or even the surfaces of Mars, Venus, and the moon). [ From the October 2021 issue: Did the first Americans arrive by land or by sea? ] When modern human beings began to move out of Africa in serious numbers, starting at least 70,000 years ago, the planet had already been cooling for some 45,000 years, and sea levels were already more than 200 feet below where they are now. During the following 50,000 years, sea levels continued to drop, which meant that as people spread across the globe, they were often moving through and settling in coastal regions of Aquaterra that are now as much as 400 feet underwater. And for much of that time, they were doing far more than just hunting and gathering. Many of the developments that have defined modern human society, Dobson argues, may have had their origins in those now-submerged lands. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” he writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.” Aquaterra therefore demands recognition—and exploration. “It was not just a place,” Dobson told me. “It was a wellspring of the human race.” Dobson has long been on something of a lonely quest to get geographers to adopt the name Aquaterra. The chance to name a giant new Earth feature doesn’t arrive often (Antarctica, one of the most recent additions, began to appear on maps in the 1880s, although the word had been around for centuries), and if that feature happens to be largely invisible, you’re likely to run into difficulties persuading others to go along with your name. Call the feature what you will, but it exists: During the past 20,000 years, huge stretches of formerly inhabited land along the world’s coastal shelves have disappeared underwater, taking with them tens of thousands of years of human history. Until recently, that is. During the past few decades, artifacts and sites dating back millennia have been found off the coasts of every inhabited continent. A growing number of researchers—geographers, archaeologists, anthropologists, amateur enthusiasts—are turning their attention to what lies offshore. “Everywhere we’ve systematically looked, we’ve found some areas where the former landscape has survived,” Jessi Halligan, an anthropologist at Texas A&M, told me. “And in a lot of those places, those former landscapes have had sites on them.” Illustration by Owen Pomery. Source: Vince Gaffney. Taken together, the lands that make up Aquaterra, in orange, amount to a mass the size of South America. The sheer range of these underwater finds is remarkable. Hand axes that are 300,000 to 1.4 million years old have turned up in the waters off South Africa. Neanderthal artifacts dating back more than 200,000 years have been found under the North Sea. In 2014 and 2015, a dredging project in Indonesia’s Madura Strait brought up a rich trove of fossils that are 120,000 to 160,000 years old, including the remains of early hominins and a host of megafaunal species. The finds that bear most directly on the modern human story, however, come from the most recent glacial cycle. In the Mediterranean, near Marseille, France, there’s Cosquer Cave , whose entrance, 120 feet below sea level, offers divers access to dry interior chambers adorned with engravings and wall paintings that date from 19,000 to 27,000 years ago. In the Baltic, near Germany, there’s the recently discovered Blinkerwall , one of Europe’s oldest and largest Stone Age structures—more than 10,000 years old and more than half a mile long—which seems to have been used as a drive lane for hunting reindeer. Off the southern coast of England, at Bouldnor Cliff , near the Isle of Wight, divers have discovered roughly 1,000 stone tools and a wealth of organic material, preserved by lack of oxygen, including fragments of worked wood, traces of food, and the oldest pieces of string ever found in Britain. There’s action across the Atlantic too. Fishermen in the Chesapeake Bay region have hauled up so many artifacts that a 2020 article in an archaeology journal organized the finds according to the means of discovery: those brought to light by shrimp trawlers, scallop dredgers, crab scrapers, or oyster tongs. There’s also activity in the Gulf of Mexico. Describing the work that she and others have done there, Jessica Cook Hale, a marine geoarchaeologist, told me, “You can’t fall off a boat in Apalachee Bay—on the east side of that bay—without bumping into a site.” Cook Hale is affiliated with the Submerged Landscapes Research Centre , at the University of Bradford, in England—an important global hub for specialists in the field. Most discoveries are made accidentally. Recreational divers pick things up. Fishing boats snag objects in their nets. Amateur collectors near The Hague, in the Netherlands, regularly find tools, fossils, and bones on the shores of the Zandmotor, an artificial peninsula created with sand vacuumed up from the seabed. At Bouldnor Cliff, divers exploring the remains of a submerged ancient forest noticed that lobsters were flinging Stone Age tools out onto the seafloor as they dug their burrows. Once sites are located, the painstaking task of exploration and excavation begins. Doing archaeology underwater poses special challenges. Limited by the amount of air in their tanks, divers have to work in short, purposeful bursts. They have to descend with special equipment: underwater writing slates, inflatable marker buoys and GPS units, pre-labeled plastic bags. There are animals to contend with: Eels defend their lairs; remoras harass you; jellyfish sting. Ocean conditions—cold water, strong currents, terrible visibility—can be tricky. Helen Farr, a maritime archaeologist at the University of Southampton, has described working in the North Sea as like “diving in cold tea.” In November 2025, I flew to London to attend a conference at the stately British Academy titled “Taken at the Flood,” which brought together many of the leading figures in the study of underwater landscapes and archaeology. We were ourselves submerged, gathered in a windowless space on what the building map referred to as the “lower ground” floor. The conference’s closing speaker was Geoff Bailey, a British archaeologist who has spent more than 50 years conducting research around the world, with a focus in recent decades on what lies underwater. His look is somehow both grizzled and dignified. In his final remarks, Bailey proposed a thought experiment: Imagine a distant future in which sea levels have risen about 200 feet—the sort of rise that might take place if Antarctica and Greenland were to lose all of their ice cover. To show us what Europe would look like with sea levels that high, he projected a map onto the wall. Britain and Ireland had been reduced to an archipelago of small islands. Northwestern Europe’s present coastlines and lowland areas lay deep underwater. Offshore, red dots lined the continent’s diminished periphery, indicating fully or partly drowned cities: London. Lisbon. Barcelona. Rome. Amsterdam. Copenhagen. In this scenario, Bailey asked, what if archaeologists of the future could study only what remained above sea level, in places that today sit well inland from the coast? If they saw no evidence of sea-based culture in the cities that survived, what would they assume about life in 21st-century Europe? “They would think it was basically land-based,” he said, “with major centers of power in Madrid, Prague, Moscow—places like that. Because all of the capital cities of Western Europe would be underwater, and most of the infrastructure that supports our present civilization.” That’s a bit of a stretch, but it does help bring into focus what’s been happening since the beginning of modern archaeology. In assembling a picture of our past, we’ve focused on what has survived on land (in the former highlands) while ignoring what lies underwater. The result is that we’ve assembled a picture of our past that is likely to be just as fragmentary and misleading as the one those future archaeologists might assemble of the world we live in today. We may have missed a lot. What we won’t ever find, however, are the ruins of a lost civilization deep under the sea. That sort of thinking, wishful and pseudoscientific, is the province of the popular British writer Graham Hancock, whose book Underworld (2002) promoted the idea that advanced seafaring civilizations flourished during the last Ice Age and were then swallowed by rising seas, leaving only enigmatic traces behind. Its popularity drives specialists in the field crazy. “Cult stuff” is how the British marine geoarchaeologist Nicholas Flemming described it to me. If the study of drowned ancient landscapes has a founding figure, it’s Flemming. Almost everybody I talked with for this article described him as a prime mover. So after the conference, I went to meet him at his home in Surrey, some 30 miles southwest of London. Flemming has had an astonishingly varied, adventurous, and productive career. It began in the 1950s, when he trained as a commando and diver with the Special Boat Service of the Royal Marines (roughly the equivalent of the Navy SEALs). He then pursued doctoral studies in oceanography at Cambridge. Over the past seven decades, Flemming has published more than 300 papers and reports and has also dived in the waters of more than 30 countries—continuing long after a car crash in the Balkans in 1969 left him paralyzed from the chest down. When diving from that point on, he used no special equipment: He swam with his arms rather than his legs and needed help only when entering and exiting the water. Flemming, who is 90, has the look of a retired British adventurer from a bygone age. His hair is white, and he wears a walrus mustache that would have done Lord Kitchener proud. Seated in his wheelchair, he greeted me in his front hall and then, wasting no time on formalities, ushered me into his study. Flemming told me about the doctoral work he’d done at Cambridge, where he studied sea-level and tectonic change in the Mediterranean by surveying Greek and Roman harbors and ancient caves. As part of that effort, he worked on hundreds of submerged sites from classical antiquity. By the early 1960s, he had developed a conviction that much older sites might have survived underwater, and that he and others could find them. Jamie Salmons for The Atlantic Nicholas Flemming, 90, has explored the waters of more than 30 countries, continuing to dive even after an accident left him partly paralyzed. Many archaeologists disagreed. Even when very old artifacts did occasionally turn up—most famously, perhaps, a 14,000-year-old deer-antler harpoon that a fishing vessel named the Colinda hauled out of the North Sea in a block of peat in 1931—they were treated as isolated curiosities. But Flemming interpreted them as confirmation that a whole drowned world of human history awaited discovery. “I knew what we were going to do and what we would find,” he told me. “And we did.” A major milestone occurred in the summer of 1967, when, swimming in shallow waters off the southern coast of Greece, Flemming came across the ruins of a 5,000-year-old town, known today as Pavlopetri, where street grids, courtyards, and multiroom buildings had all survived. Archaeologists use a variety of techniques to date such sites: the reconstruction of ancient sea levels; the dating of the sediment layers in which the sites are found; comparisons of pottery, tool, and architectural styles to those that have been found on land; the radiocarbon dating of any surviving organic materials. Pavlopetri remains the oldest planned town ever found underwater. In the decade that followed, Flemming continued searching for older sites. And in 1981, off a small island called Aghios Petros , he discovered the remnants of a nearly 8,000-year-old village. As he described it in his 2021 memoir, Apollonia on My Mind , the Neolithic villagers had picked an “ideal spot”—the underwater site, bordering a sheltered inlet and supplied with a freshwater spring, would once have stood on a peninsula that reached into the bay. Others were making discoveries too. From 1978 to 1988, the Danish archaeologist Søren H. Andersen led intensive excavations in the Baltic Sea at the submerged settlement site of Tybrind Vig—excavations that yielded a wealth of preserved organic materials, many of them more than 7,000 years old, including canoes, decorated wooden paddles, fishing gear, bone tools, and plant remains. In 1984, while doing routine survey work in the Mediterranean, near Haifa, the Israeli marine archaeologist Ehud Galili discovered a site now known as Atlit-Yam: a 9,000-year-old submerged village of extraordinary completeness. It had houses, wells, and evidence of agriculture and ritual activity, including human burials. By the early ’80s, Flemming was beginning to feel less drawn to the study of classical sites. He’d worked on hundreds, after all. “Okay, they’re very visual,” he told me. “They’re pretty. But one more Roman port?” Much older archaeology was what interested Flemming now—the “big game,” as he put it. “You could have Neanderthals living on the seafloor,” he remembered thinking. “You could have had elephants and rhinoceroses wandering on the floor of the North Sea and the Mediterranean.” At the time, Geoff Bailey was starting to have similar thoughts. He’d begun his career in the 1970s by studying evidence of ancient coastal settlement. In particular, he studied accumulations of discarded shells, or shell middens, tens of thousands of which survive along the world’s coastlines, some of them hundreds of feet long and dozens of feet high. The layers of shells, piled up after their contents were eaten, preserve long records of human activity, including flaked stone, bone tools, the charcoal of old hearths, and sometimes evidence of human burials. Such sites began to appear in large numbers about 6,000 to 7,000 years ago, just as sea levels were gradually stabilizing—around where they are now. In the ’70s, most archaeologists thought the explanation for this phenomenon was straightforward. While sea levels were rising, the theory went, coastal regions were simply changing too much to have supported the range of human activities associated with social complexity. But once sea levels settled, a sort of postglacial revolution ensued. “Boom!” Bailey said, describing that view to me. “Suddenly you’ve got this explosion of shell mounds, coastal settlements, fishing technology, dugout canoes, etc., all over the world.” Bailey entertained doubts about that story early on. It seemed far more likely to him that people had been exploiting coastal environments, which are rich in resources and easy to move around in, for much longer than just the past 6,000 years or so. Wouldn’t it make more sense, he thought, if the “sudden” emergence of cultural complexity along the world’s coasts was simply a reflection of where and when the seas had stopped rising—and stopped covering up all the earlier coastal communities? Archaeologists, he felt, had fallen prey to evidentiary misdirection: The remains of communities on high ground had survived, whereas the original coastal communities had been washed away. Owen Pomery Others were pursuing related ideas. In 1975, the archaeologist Michael Moseley published The Maritime Foundations of Andean Civilization , in which he argued that much of the social complexity of ancient Peru arose along the coast, primarily powered not by agriculture, as was generally believed, but by the biological richness of the sea. All of these ideas had important implications. If tens of thousands of years ago, people were living in significant numbers in coastal areas, they almost surely developed seafaring technologies and sophisticated navigational know-how long before we see any trace of such things in the terrestrial record. That would have enabled them to make longer and longer excursions at sea—to fish, to trade, or just to explore. To the underwater archaeologist George Bass, there was an obvious lesson in all of this, one that would help explain how people were able to spread so rapidly across the globe after migrating out of Africa. “Before there were either farmers or shepherds,” he wrote, “there were sailors.” The study of submerged prehistory started with a relatively amateur focus on artifacts and has progressed to the scientific examination of sites. At the turn of the 21st century, a new phase began: the reconstruction of entire lost landscapes. A major force behind this development was the English archaeologist Bryony Coles, who, while a professor at the University of Exeter in the 1990s, decided that she was tired of hearing people talk about the “land bridge” that had once connected Great Britain to continental Europe. By that point, enough artifacts had emerged from the North Sea, and enough was known about sea-level change during the glacial cycle, to suggest a very different picture. The North Sea basin had once been a fertile lowland, home to all sorts of plants and animals—and people. The whole area had been a place to be , it seemed to Coles, not just a place to cross . During that time, Coles made a ferry journey from Britain to Sweden, which took her over a large, shallow feature of the seafloor known as the Dogger Bank. That crossing gave her an idea: To help dispel the land-bridge notion, why not borrow from the name Dogger Bank and call the whole submerged landscape Doggerland? And why not try to reconstruct what it used to look like? Coles read everything she could find about seafloor terrain, sea-level change, artifacts and animal bones hauled up by fishing vessels, and the archaeology of adjacent coastal regions. In 1998, she published a paper—“Doggerland: A Speculative Survey”—that included a series of maps presenting Doggerland’s landscape during different stages of the glacial cycle. In Coles’s reconstruction, Doggerland had evolved from a near-empty polar desert at the height of glaciation (some 18,000 years ago) into a grassland of birch and willow grazed by mammoths, horses, and elk (as temperatures rose), then into a forested expanse of hazel and oak cut by big rivers and estuaries, and finally (by about 7,000 years ago) into a scattering of islands in the midst of the encroaching North Sea—the largest of which, now submerged, we know as the Dogger Bank. Coles’s paper sparked a conceptual revolution: Doggerland was a real place. A few years after Coles published her article, Vince Gaffney, a British landscape archaeologist then at the University of Birmingham, and two colleagues, Ken Thomson and Simon Fitch, started to wonder: Might any of the companies that were prospecting for oil and gas deposits under the North Sea floor be willing to share the survey data they’d been gathering? It was a clever idea. By using the bounce-back of sound waves to identify features and anomalies deep below the seafloor—so-called seismic-reflection surveys—the companies had developed 3-D maps of the basin that were unparalleled in detail and scope. Gaffney and his colleagues suspected that those maps might include information about Doggerland. One company, Petroleum Geo-Services, agreed to share some of its information, and once the archaeologists began analyzing the data, translated on-screen, they discerned the beds of an ancient river and its tributaries. “I just looked at it,” Gaffney told me, “and thought, Bloody hell, this is going to work .” He and his colleagues soon reconstructed a 25-mile stretch of the river, which they determined had been almost the size of the Rhine. In the decades since, Gaffney and his team—now based at the Submerged Landscapes Research Centre—have reconstructed more than 40,000 square miles of Doggerland. “If you put a line from Yorkshire to Denmark,” Gaffney said, “pretty much everything below that was at some point dry land, and we have largely mapped that area.” That makes Doggerland by far the most extensively studied “paleo-landscape” in the world. “What this is,” Jonathan Benjamin told me, holding a large, greenish lump of rock in his hand, “is a beautiful hafted axe.” Benjamin was speaking via videochat from Australia, where he is a professor of maritime archaeology at Flinders University. He held the rock up to his computer so I could make a closer examination. To me, it looked more like a vaguely deformed mango than an axe, but Benjamin quickly helped me see it for what it was. He told me to imagine his forearm as a handle—the “haft”—and he then rotated the rock in his hand until I was looking at one of its narrow sides. All of a sudden, I saw an expertly tapered blade at the head of an axe—one that had lain underwater for millennia. Benjamin chopped at me from half a world away. “It’s still sharp,” he said. That axe is just one of more than 260 Stone Age artifacts that Benjamin and his team discovered in 2019 , in the shallow waters around Murujuga, part of the Dampier Archipelago, off Australia’s northwestern coast. This was the first site of such antiquity securely documented in tropical waters. News of the discovery thrilled Nic Flemming, who had been arguing for decades that such sites would be found. In fact, back in 1982, with his infant daughter in tow, he had led a month-long survey of the Cootamundra Shoal, about 200 miles off Australia’s northern coast. The expedition, searching for ancient occupied terrain, was the first of its kind. Flemming didn’t expect to find any archaeological remains during this short outing, but he and his team were able to confirm that the conditions in the area were, as he put it in his memoir, “sufficient to support a Palaeolithic ice age human population during periods of low sea level.” Benjamin and his team, aware of that work, had found their site by means of logical deduction. For years, they had conducted sophisticated survey work, using sonar, seafloor mapping, aerial imagery, and paleo-environmental modeling to identify promising areas for investigation. By 2019, they had narrowed down their target area so precisely that when they began diving, they quickly found what they were looking for: ancient stone tools and environmental evidence of a once-inhabited landscape. In 2025, they went prospecting again and found more stone tools, dating back at least 9,000 years. “We keep finding more sites,” Benjamin said. “Sites that make us ask even more questions.” Benjamin’s team does its work in partnership with the Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation, which represents the traditional owners of the lands in that part of Australia. In recent years, it has become clear that the flood myths and stories that have been told for millennia by Indigenous peoples all over the world, often dismissed as primitive, fanciful, or at best symbolic, might encode historically accurate memories of past landscapes and areas of habitation in submerged regions of Aquaterra. Malik Churnside, an Aboriginal park ranger trained by Benjamin and his team so that he could take part in a recent dive, put this idea to me straightforwardly. Describing one of the tools that he’d found during a dive, he said, “It’s literally picking up pieces of history from these old stories from way back in the day.” Nowhere is there a richer surviving body of such history than in Australia, where some traditional Aboriginal stories contain references to a now-drowned land known as Sea Country. Acknowledging this ancient oral history, Benjamin and his collaborators have named their research initiative “Deep History of Sea Country.” Patrick Nunn, a geographer at the University of the Sunshine Coast, in Queensland, has devoted years to studying the ways in which some Aboriginal traditions preserve memories of coastal change. If a story refers to an identifiable landscape feature that’s now underwater, Nunn and his colleagues then use what they know about the history of the terrain and sea-level rise in that area to determine how long ago that feature must have been drowned—which in turn provides them with a minimum age for the story. To date, Nunn and his colleagues have identified 35 areas along the coast of Australia where Indigenous traditions preserve accurate memories of what Sea Country was like when it was land. The oldest stories, Nunn told me, concern the submergence of the Bass Strait “land bridge,” between the island of Tasmania and the Australian mainland, roughly 12,000 years ago. That’s a long way back. So far back, in fact, that, if Nunn is correct, these accounts may be the earliest surviving record of human experience, sitting right at what he calls “the edge of memory.” Few of the sites that have been found in Aquaterra date back beyond 10,000 years. That’s starting to change as scanning and seabed-coring technologies improve, submersible drones become affordable, and industry data become more readily available. Geographers and archaeologists have now named Ice Age landmasses whose drowned lowlands dwarf even those of Doggerland. Between Siberia and Alaska, there’s Beringia, whose submerged portion is roughly the size of Greenland. Connecting Australia, New Guinea, and Tasmania, there’s Sahul, whose submerged portion is nearly twice the size of the Iberian Peninsula. And connecting mainland Southeast Asia with Sumatra, Java, and Borneo, there’s Sundaland, whose submerged portion is roughly a quarter the size of Australia. Those regions are now all understood to have been complex lowland ecosystems that for tens of thousands of years were home to all manner of flora and fauna. Their drowned portions are virtually unexplored—and all undoubtedly contain sites and fossils and landscapes that can help us answer big questions about human origins, global migration, and cultural development. Cultural treasures might also await discovery. To imagine the possibilities, consider by analogy some of the great treasures found on land from our deep past: the lion-man of Hohlenstein-Stadel (roughly 40,000 years old), the astonishing art in Chauvet Cave (roughly 36,000 years old), the Venus of Willendorf (roughly 29,000 years old), the monumental Göbekli Tepe site (more than 10,000 years old). All were created at times when global sea levels were roughly 150 to 300 feet lower than they are today, in regions that lay considerably farther from the world’s coasts than they now do. If many people—probably most people—during those same eras lived in coastal regions, as people from every era always have, they will have left extraordinary things behind. Aquaterra has not only a past but also a future. As sea levels rise, Geoff Bailey’s thought experiment is worth revisiting. If, over thousands of years, global warming were to melt our remaining ice sheets, the world’s oceans might rise another 200 feet. That would mean the drowning of another whole continent’s worth of land—and, once again, we’d lose coastal regions where much of human history and development has played out. Bailey focused on Europe in his thought experiment, but with sea levels that much higher, many great cities all over the world would disappear. North America would lose New York, Miami, New Orleans, Houston, and Boston, among many others. In South America, Buenos Aires and Rio de Janeiro would go under; Africa would lose Lagos, Cairo, and much of Cape Town. Huge Asian population centers—Mumbai, Bangkok, Tokyo, Singapore, Jakarta, Shanghai—would drown, as would Darwin and Brisbane, in Australia. [ From the July/August 2024 issue: A wild plan to avert catastrophic sea-level rise ] The contours of the United States would be transformed. Florida would largely disappear. The Piedmont would become the country’s new east coast. Submerged monuments and memorials in Washington, D.C., might become popular dive spots. The Gulf of Mexico would fill in much of the Mississippi Valley. In California, an inland sea might spread into the Central Valley, drowning Sacramento and Stockton and almost reaching Fresno. The point isn’t to lament that such things might happen. It’s to illustrate how skewed perceptions of our era would be if all of this terrain were removed from future consciousness. And that, in turn, is a reminder that exploring Aquaterra could help us answer some of the great open questions about our past. When did people first leave Africa, and how did they make their way to Southeast Asia? How did people cross open water and reach Australia in numbers significant enough to settle there? No evidence survives of the boats and technologies that made those migrations possible, because many of the coastal regions where they were developed today lie deep underwater in Sundaland and Sahul. And what about the Americas? Did the first people to reach them live for millennia in the now-drowned landscapes of Beringia? Did they use watercraft to make their way along the now-drowned western coasts of North and South America? The objects and sites that can help answer such questions may well exist on, and only on, the world’s submerged continental shelves. We live in an anomalous era. Aquaterra may be mostly water today, but for the greater part of human history—indeed, for the greater part of the past million years—it was mostly land. And that land is where we came from. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “The Lost World of Aquaterra.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

items.title: What I Learned About Christmas—And Life—By Starring* in a Hallmark Movie
items.description: Photographs by Sophie Green On a Hallmark movie set, it is always Christmas but rarely winter. When you produce dozens of original holiday movies a year, there is only so much year for filming, and so you often find yourself making Christmas in July. As I am doing now in Canterbury, England. It doesn’t reliably snow in Canterbury anymore, even in actual winter, but there is snow on the ground. A man from Snowboy Systems, a producer of artificial snow from the East Midlands, is hosing down the sidewalk; the artificial snow on the sidewalk looks less artificial, he says, when the sidewalk is damp. This sidewalk snow is made from biodegradable paper and has the consistency of wet string cheese. Lining the sides of the cathedral are long strips of fleecy, fluffy artificial snow, like the kind in a department-store window. We are setting up for the big final kiss in the snow—a Hallmark Christmas needs a big final kiss in the snow—and that snow, falling from on high, will be made of foam. Three different types of fake snow in a single day of filming! That is what I’m here to study: how to make something so expertly fake that it feels real. The Hallmark Channel turned 25 this year, and the brand is strong—so strong that specifying “Hallmark Christmas movie” feels redundant. On weekends from mid-October through December 2025, more U.S. women were watching Hallmark’s programming than that of all other cable networks, including news and sports, according to Hallmark. Over that period as a whole, Hallmark was the second-most-watched cable network among women, behind only Fox News Channel (do you prefer countdowns to Christmas, or wars on Christmas?). Sophie Green for The Atlantic The team from Snowboy Systems prepares Canterbury Cathedral for fake snowfall. Netflix is now in the holiday-movie game with steamier concepts such as Hot Frosty , in which a snowman becomes a man with washboard abs. And short Christmas movies are being made just for your phone, in vertical-video form. Have you seen Found a Homeless Billionaire Husband for Christmas on ReelShort, a platform for “microdramas”? The 71 episodes are each less than two minutes long; this microdrama is not even trying to have realistic fake snow. My social-media feeds are now garlanded with AI Christmas videos that purport to be time capsules of the 1970s or ’80s, showing sweater-clad families laughing as their turkey materializes out of thin air. Congratulations, we used all the water that formerly became snow to give you this creepy, plotless fauxstalgia! Hallmark, despite the available technology, is still something made by humans for humans. The snow may be fake, but at least the fake snow is real. There is something tremendous about being among people who, using three-dimensional matter, make things nice for a living. Washington, D.C., where I live, and the world, where I also live, have both felt not nice lately. Sometimes you want to climb into a Hallmark movie. So I am at Canterbury Cathedral—mere feet from where the English archbishop Thomas Becket was stabbed by the knights of Henry II—to be a Passerby and a Concert Attendee in a fetching winter coat. But, as with all things made by humans, there is an element of unpredictability. While on set, I receive word that I have been promoted. I will not just be a Passerby. I will not just be a Concert Attendee. I will be Lord Mayor of Canterbury. Lord Mayor of Canterbury does not sound like an ornament on the side of the tree that faces the wall. Lord Mayor of Canterbury sounds like someone who’s actually in this movie—who may, in fact, have to act , for real. And this is when, under my fetching winter coat, I start to sweat. In the beginning, we had winter but no Christmas. Then, during the reign of Roman Emperor Augustus, someone named Jesus was born. It took a while for news of this event to spread, and still longer for this event to become a holiday. Celebrations really got into gear in the fourth century, after Constantine converted to Christianity. By the 12th century, the holiday had sprawled into a period of wassail drinking and jubilant misrule; in some churches, a choirboy was made a fake bishop and allowed to give a sermon. Becket himself gave the Christmas sermon in 1170; the stabbing, on the future Hallmark set, happened four days later. There were a few evolutionary hops between vassals wassailing and American families zoning out in front of their TV sets, and many of them happened in the 19th century: Charles Dickens’s ghost story staved Christmas into a beloved fable of generosity, and The Nutcracker turned the holiday into a hallucinatory nightmare. The 20th century gave us Bing Crosby’s workhorse playlist, The Muppet Christmas Carol , and Mariah Carey’s jingle-jangling anthem of the pining heart. And on August 5, 2001, along came the Hallmark Channel, which gift wrapped two millennia of scattered ritual and merriment into a digestible box the size of our TV screens. Its “Countdown to Christmas” helped cement the holi day as a holi season , which lately begins before Halloween. Turn on your TV at any point during this time and see the modern image of Christmas: a man in a turtleneck sweater kissing a self-possessed heroine in the falling snow. Before Hallmark, what original TV movies could you watch in the Christmas season? The landscape was pretty dismal. Consider the TV listings for December 2000. There were just a handful of holiday-movie premieres, including Special Delivery , with Andy Dick, and VH1’s A Diva’s Christmas Carol , with Vanessa Williams as Ebony Scrooge. On Fox Family, you could catch an airing of 1996’s The Angel of Pennsylvania Avenue , in which three children try to get President Hoover ( President Hoover? ) to pardon their wrongfully convicted father in time for Christmas. But even Hallmark took a little while to find its stride, as anyone who has watched the 2003 classic A Carol Christmas can attest. Have you ever wanted to see Gary Coleman, William Shatner, and (an uncredited) James Cromwell play the ghosts of Christmases past, present, and future? Or hear Tori Spelling utter the Dickensian paraphrase “I’m gonna hold Christmas in my heart”? Run, don’t walk, to rent this gem. But then, in 2006, we got The Christmas Card . This is the Hallmark Christmas blueprint, and it is in every way a perfect film. The stereotypical Hallmark-movie plot can sound a bit dystopian: “She was a busy woman from the big city. Then one day the snow trapped her in Christmasville, and she never left …” The Christmas Card inverts this paradigm. Our protagonist, Faith, already lives in a small town. What’s more, she loves this town, and her job at the family lumber mill, more than anything—a fact that is lost on her absentee city-slicker boyfriend, Paul, an international wine broker in a tiny sports car. But, fortunately, Faith has sent a Christmas card to a soldier named Cody, stationed in Afghanistan, and Cody is so charmed by the card that when he gets a break from fighting the War on Terror, he visits her town. He then saves Faith’s dad from an out-of-control speeding car and starts helping at the lumber business. He also picks her up in a sleigh—with her favorite blanket. Wine Broker Paul does not stand a chance. There’s an exquisite scene where Paul spends two hours in the woods yelling into his cellphone about wine while, behind him, Cody takes down Christmas trees with a chainsaw. As with any great romance, this one makes you like the lead characters instantly and then spend the next 90 minutes shouting, “NO! DON’T MARRY PAUL! ALL HE CARES ABOUT IS RIESLINGS!” Faith’s dad tells Cody that he needs someone to come back to, from the War on Terror, and this movie is about exactly that: the joy of returning to the cozy and familiar. By the end of the movie, you are frothing at the mouth lest something prevent Faith and her soldier beau, who have identical diner orders , from getting together. And of course they do, with a kiss in the snow. You can see why this masterpiece spawned a whole genre, and a legion of fans. My own mother, who initially refused to be quoted on the record for this article, is one of these fans. But can she remember the name of even one Hallmark movie? Absolutely not. It feels almost rude to ask—like demanding that a fan of winter name a favorite snowflake. The point is not the snowflake (which is unique and exquisite). The point is the flurry, and its overall effect. Does my mother love Hallmark movies individually? Yes. But what she really loves is being surrounded by them all . She is watching one right now, as I type this. (It is August.) The flurry blurs everything together. In addition to A Carol Christmas , there is It’s Christmas, Carol! (with Carrie Fisher! though not as Carol). Then there’s Time for Me to Come Home for Christmas . Time for You to Come Home for Christmas . Time for Us to Come Home for Christmas . Time for Him to Come Home for Christmas . (These are all real. It’s a franchise.) Time for Her to Come Home for Christmas . Time for Them to Come Home for Christmas . To me, this implies the existence of a more sinister Time for It to Come Home for Christmas (tagline, from Yeats: “What rough beast, its hour come round at last, slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?”). An unofficial list on IMDb counts 507 Hallmark Christmas movies, from the highest-rated, A Biltmore Christmas (2023), in which a magic hourglass whirls our heroine back to the 1940s, to the lowest-rated, A Christmas Wedding Tail (2011), with Jay Mohr voicing a Labrador named Rusty. (That list of 507 includes several Hanukkah films and a Kwanzaa film.) This year, “Countdown to Christmas” will feature 34 new movies (a Hallmark record). The flurry is now a blizzard, blanketing our screens with mass-produced mirth and brand partnerships—with the NFL ( Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story ) and Disney World (what if we locked eyes in the hall of animatronic presidents?). But the key ingredient will always be Christmas, which is an “emotional intensifier” in both Hallmark movies and real life, according to the historian Gerry Bowler, who once wrote a biography of Santa Claus. “We spend maybe 10 percent of our lives under the sway of Christmas,” he told me. “Whether you observe it or not, you have to live in it. It is the one time of the year in which we take magic seriously.” We act nicely, he says, and expect others to act nicely. So, in May, I sent a couple of emails to the Hallmark publicity team saying it was my dream to write a feature about being an extra in a Hallmark movie. They responded: Can you be in the U.K. in July? Good news! Maria, the publicist who arranges my Hallmark debut, says she’s read the script for Christmas in Canterbury and “LOVED it.” It is inspired by a true event: the first performance by a girls’ choir at Canterbury Cathedral, which happened in, amazingly, 2014. One of the producers, Oneida Crawford, saw the news and instantly thought: This miniature feminist triumph deserves to be a Hallmark movie. Sophie Green for The Atlantic The author, dressed as Lord Mayor, carries her humbler Passerby costume. Sophie Green for The Atlantic The actor Nigel Pilkington ( far left ) engages the author ( second from right ) before the cameras start rolling for the climactic choral sequence. The Hallmark heroine in Christmas in Canterbury is played by Jessy Schram, blond and blue-eyed and so iridescently sunny that you want to bend over backwards to do nice things for her. This is not her first time being a Hallmark heroine. Remember Time for Them to Come Home for Christmas ? She played a woman who, despite amnesia from a bridge-related head injury, is so iridescently sunny that everyone wants to bend over backwards to do nice things for her. Hallmark heroines are a very specific sort of person. They are “smart” and “relatable” and have “1,000-watt smiles” but are “no shrinking poinsettias,” according to the book Hallmark Channel Countdown to Christmas: Celebrate the Movie Magic (Revised Edition) , whose cover promises “Recipes, Watch Party Games & More.” Will Kemp is the Hallmark gentleman in Christmas in Canterbury (he’s also a producer). Besides starring in a substantial number of Hallmark movies, including A Not So Royal Christmas and Christmas Waltz , he was featured in The Scorpion King 4: Quest for Power , which I have not seen but does not sound like a Christmas movie. Will is English, has stunningly green eyes, and looks like he moisturizes exactly the right amount. And then there are the Hallmark extras, or background actors. In The Christmas Card , the extras buy Christmas trees from Cody, sit in church pews, and attend a dance at a veterans’ hall. In Time for Them to Come Home for Christmas , they walk through town in their winter coats, listen to street performers play the theme song, and then normalize dancing along. They populate the world of Hallmark and make it more real, yet they never draw attention to themselves. The most I have thought about Hallmark extras is: What a nice winter coat. But not as nice as the heroine’s! Now I need to think about how to be an extra. So I call up an acting coach named Mary Malaney and ask for advice. “I will be dressed as though it is winter, and so I will be very hot,” I tell Mary. “Do you know how to act cool?” Mary has detailed, smart advice about using my sense memories of moving through city streets in winter, thinking about how I would hold my arms close to my sides and keep my head down to avoid the wind. I furiously take notes. “I also have to attend a concert,” I tell her. Easy, Mary says. “If you hear something really beautiful, just allow yourself to hear it. And enjoy. And whatever is on your face in that moment is truth.” “How ambitious of a backstory can I do?” I ask. “What if I’m, like, the ghost of Thomas Becket and I’ve come back to haunt the cathedral?” “Maybe not in this instance,” Mary says. “Part of being in an ensemble of any kind is knowing how you serve the story. And unfortunately in this one, Alexandra, you are probably not the main character.” Extras are supposed to bring their own costumes, so Publicist Maria sends me a mood board of outfits for each of my two characters: Concert Attendee and Passerby. Concertgoers should bring burgundies, creams and whites, forest greens, deep reds, beiges, or other “rich winter tones,” and are to “dress smart, elegant, and subtly festive.” Passersby are instructed to avoid “modern sportswear, activewear, or trainers.” I borrow a magnificent black-and-red-checked coat from a friend with actual taste. I bring boots with heels, even though I hate wearing heels and will be miserable. The boots look wintry, and the suffering will give me character, whatever that character turns out to be. But wardrobe prep is not enough. I need Hallmark wisdom too, from the woman who wrote that perfect blueprint, The Christmas Card . “Where I live now, you can’t swing a candy cane without hitting a Christmas-tree farm,” Joany Kane says on the phone from her home in Western Massachusetts. Although she still mentors aspiring Hallmark screenwriters, Joany’s main focus these days is Wicked Merry, an original pirate-romance universe inspired, in part, by her love of Jimmy Buffett. (Volume three of her Aargh Is for Romance book series is titled If Hallmark Movies Had Pirates .) “It always seemed to me that Christmas is the best time for romance, even better than Valentine’s Day,” Joany tells me. “Valentine’s Day is kind of a made-up holiday, but Christmas is all about hope and magic.” What makes a good Christmas movie? Romance, of course. “I tend to go for swoon,” Joany says. She isn’t into death or trauma. She wants her lead characters to lock eyes and feel something. “Like in The King and I , when he just puts his hand on her waist when they’re dancing? And he pulls her close? Oh my gosh, I just live for those moments. Every single script I write, I write around How can I get to this moment? ” A moment of swoon. Whatever is on your face in that moment is truth. All I have to do in Canterbury is be in the moment and respond as a normal human would. Doing things with my body, like a person. But anyone who knows me will tell you: This is not where I excel. Canterbury is a beautiful old English cathedral city. Charles Dickens liked it so much that he set some of David Copperfield in it. The Nazis disliked it so much that they destroyed a chunk of it during the Baedeker Blitz. Today, you can eat at a pub named the Old Weavers House that has been around longer than the city of Cleveland. You can go punting on a trout-filled river past a former priory that was built before the Aztec empire. And you can have fish and chips with Publicist Maria and then walk to a real Canterbury street where the magic—the niceness—is under way. Sophie Green for The Atlantic The stars of Christmas in Canterbury , Jessy Schram and Will Kemp, sit ensconced in wool and plaid—two crucial Hallmark ingredients.
