This is day 13 of the 15-day shoot (a typical length for a Hallmark production). The crew has been through a lot together, including choir rehearsals with children and a July heat dome. This film has been shot in roughly chronological order, meaning that tomorrow will be the first half of the climax, a choral concert where I will play Concert Attendee. And day 15 will feature the big final kiss in the snow. (Spoiler alert! Indeed, everything that follows—and some of what precedes—contains mild spoilers for Christmas in Canterbury , which airs December 11.) Have you ever thought, Theater is fine, but what I really want is to watch just one little scene entirely liberated from its context, eight or nine times in a row. Each time should be slightly different, but also very hard to hear, and there should be a man holding a boom mic standing in the way ? If so, you will love being on a movie set. This particular set is a scenic lane of colorful rowhouses all playing themselves. A light on a cherry picker illuminates the street from above, making this entire block look like it is being abducted by a UFO. The night is quiet and pleasant, but punctuated by bursts of joy or distress from a neighboring pub (the World Cup semifinal is on). Will Kemp is about to walk Jessy Schram to her door, where they will no doubt want to kiss but refrain from doing so, because the climactic choral scene has not happened yet. I don’t have access to the script, so I can only guess the plot from the snippets of dialogue I hear and the broad outline from Publicist Maria: Jessy Schram is Rose, a choir director from Vienna, Ohio. After her beloved Grandma Bud dies, she leaves home looking for adventure. She travels to Canterbury and stays with her heavily pregnant friend, who is a choir director for girls. When this friend becomes too pregnant to direct, Rose is asked to fill in—because everyone thinks she’s an esteemed choir director from Vienna, Austria . She meets the straitlaced Harrison (Will Kemp), who is also a choir director—for boys . While competing for the coveted Christmas Eve concert slot, Hallmark heroine and Hallmark gentleman feel a spark that inspires them to merge their choirs . But no merging has yet taken place. So, tonight, Will walks Jessy home to her door (blue, with a Christmas wreath on it). They are discussing whether their night was an adventure? (It’s hard to hear.) Yes, Jessy says, “because we kept our hearts open.” They do multiple takes. John Barrymore allegedly called love “the delightful interval between meeting a beautiful girl and discovering she looks like a haddock”; similarly, I feel that takes two through nine are the interval between marveling at the heartfelt dialogue and doubting that any human being would ever say these words in this order. But Jessy and Will are making it work. And so are the extras. Two extras walk through the scene, arm in arm, on an unerring path just where the camera needs them to be. I watch them in awe. They appear to be chatting naturally, yet they make no sound. Remarkable. Tomorrow, this is going to be my job. “Because we both kept our hearts open,” Jessy says again, warmly. Between takes, the team from Snowboy sprays down the street. “Because we both kept our hearts open,” Jessy says yet again, flirtier this time. She exudes Hallmark energy from every pore. At one point she will curse in front of the children’s choir and immediately revise “FUCK!” to “BUCKETS FULL OF CHRISTMAS!” Even the curses are festive here. That’s how deep the nice is on a Hallmark set. It is so deep that Will Kemp is looking for ways to help people “level up” in all parts of the production. This, apparently, includes me. Before I leave set for the night, he tells me I’ve been promoted to Lord Mayor of Canterbury. I will ease into that illustrious station via my first on-camera appearance as a humble Passerby outside the cathedral. (Or am I the Lord Mayor, walking among the people? I am never certain of the answer to this question, so I decide to play Lord Mayor and Passerby as two distinct characters, to show my range.) A shuttle brings us extras to a building full of chairs and tents that serve as changing rooms. There is also a costume rack and a hair-and-makeup area near the window. The first step for extras (called “supporting artists” in the U.K.) is to show the outfits that we have brought, for approval or rejection by the costume team. The team goes into British raptures over my borrowed black-and-red coat, in the sense that they tell me I have “fit the brief.” I am surrounded by other extras, and quickly share their conviction that this is one of the most exciting jobs on Earth. There is Helen, a model, who became a supporting artist because Ridley Scott’s Napoleon needed people for an orgy scene. She says the filmmakers decided to go with younger extras for the orgy (rude!), but this near miss got her into the casting database, and she has been having a blast in the background ever since. “You’ll actually find the background is where the interest is,” Helen says. “Without the background, you have no texture.” Chloe, a Hallmark superfan and certified “Kemper,” is appearing in this movie because Will Kemp messaged her on Instagram and invited her to do so. “I probably sound obsessed,” she says apologetically, after telling me that she has attended six straight Christmas Cons, has been on two Hallmark cruises, and has a tattoo of the Hallmark crown logo on her arm. What is it about Hallmark that she loves so much? “It’s such a community,” she says. “And even the stars, they are so nice.” Articulating what makes Hallmark magical is indeed tough. Even my mother, with whom I’ve watched so many of these movies, can only offer: “They are predictably upbeat, generally enjoyable, and feature a suite of actors who become familiar faces over time.” Generally enjoyable? As a Star Wars nut myself, I have less difficulty explaining my fandom. “It’s a multigenerational, modern-day myth,” I would say about Star Wars . It’s life, but space . Something similar can be said of Hallmark, which is its own genre of mythology: life, but nice . It’s life, but with someone helping you out of a sleigh in a gentlemanly manner. It is time to become a Passerby. The assistant directors herd us to the flagstone streets, where we will be captured for posterity walking into the cathedral, then sitting in the cathedral. It is balmy. I am comfortable in my coat and white knit hat, complete with a pom-pom. First, we have a five-second establishing shot of people walking into the cathedral. Simple! All I have to do is walk in a normal manner. Someone shouts at me—I think it is the third assistant director, but I am too excited to be sure—to look up at the cathedral mid-walk, as a person might do. So I put my hands on my hips and tilt my whole body up to the sky like a little teapot. I know that this is not correct, but I have more pressing problems: I have forgotten how to walk. I have the strong sense that it involves my feet, but what if that’s wrong? Maybe it’s some kind of hop? And do you swing your arms while you do it? No, that can’t be. I am being a marionette instead of a person. This take was either so good or so bad that they do not ask me to do more of them. “I feel like you just forget how to walk, don’t you?” says Nathan, a fellow supporting artist. “I’ve done so many scenes, like, walking down stairs, and that’s the worst for me.” It is amazing how you can do any action hundreds or thousands of times without thinking about it, and the second you have to do it for an audience, you become a hapless lump attempting to walk on dry land for the first time. Next I have to be two things I’ve never been—a lord and a mayor— simultaneously . What if she, too, has to walk? My acting experience is somewhat limited. In my youth, I tended to play numbered parts rather than named parts: 23rd Cousin A in a middle-school production called The Land of the Dragon (there was also a 23rd Cousin B who repeated my lines after I said them), and Puck 2 (or possibly 3) of an unspecified number of Pucks at Shakespeare summer camp. So I would describe my acting level as “exactly correct for a production where many of the featured extras are friends or relatives of the producer.” You see me perform and think, Now, that’s someone who was available on the date they were filming . But there aren’t three Lord Mayors, or even two. There is one. Sophie Green for The Atlantic The author as Lord Mayor of Canterbury, standing completely normally I email my acting coach in a panic. Due to the time difference, I don’t hear back from her immediately. Instead, I study famous mayors. I pull up Rudy Giuliani and Fiorello La Guardia on my phone. There are many pictures of Fiorello La Guardia standing behind a desk looking like a fish who is about to burst into song. I try to replicate these mayoral expressions. I also email the actual Lord Mayor of Canterbury, a man named Alister Brady whose photo and contact information I find online: “Do you have any advice for someone who wants to wordlessly convey the essence of Mayor of Canterbury?” Amazingly, I get no response to this email. My Lord Mayor outfit includes not a sash but a chain of office, which a costumer carefully stitches onto my costume blazer. Although the chain has a large, sparkling red jewel that vaguely resembles the Eye of Sauron, the accessory is, on closer inspection, held together by a safety pin. My fellow extra Natalie says that viewers will call me the “Temu Mayor,” and I am not sure she’s wrong. Maybe the mayor sold her real chain of office to pay for choir music? (This is me doing character work.) Natalie says she played a dwarf in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power , complete with dwarf ears, so she knows what a powerful talisman should look like. I get myself into costume, trying to remain calm. Speaking of Natalies, Natalie Portman has said that scents help her get into character. Well, I have brought a scent with me: Dove’s Cinnamon Pumpkin Pie deodorant, a product that exists. Thanks to this product, my armpits smell like someone is cooking Thanksgiving dinner in them. Hopefully, this will add a subtle sense of festivity to all of the mayor’s interactions. Hair and makeup’s vision for the Lord Mayor is hair pulled back into a severe bun with what feels like 800 hairpins, and no makeup. “I think the Lord Mayor might wear mascara,” I say timidly, and they gently apply some. The photographer documenting my experience wants to take a portrait of me in my mayor outfit. This takes longer than it should. “Stand normally,” she urges. Unfortunately, I have never in my life stood normally and am not about to break this habit for her. Also, I cannot stop bursting into laughter. “You know, the forbidden laugh,” I say to her, as if this explains anything. Listen. I have a lifelong condition that causes me to react to serious situations with compounding fits of laughter. In dancing school, I had to write a letter of apology for destroying a lecture with the giggles. I once went to a wedding where the officiant surprised the bride and groom with an arts-and-crafts project during the vows. As the couple began cutting hearts out of red construction paper, I began shaking with laughter, then weeping with laughter. Fortunately, you are supposed to cry at weddings. “It’s just so beautiful,” I managed, through my sobs. (If you are reading this, Chris, it was a lovely wedding, really.) We receive the call to set, which is the actual cathedral, playing itself, but nicer. The cathedral choir looks beautiful, thanks to the lighting team and the strategic placement of dozens of fake candles. The job of Concert Attendee would have been just to sit there, take it in, and applaud at the end. The Lord Mayor’s role is somewhat more involved. Everything , it turns out, hinges on the mayor—and on her ability to make a normal face. “You’re the mayor?” asks a man with a mustache. He moves to sit next to me, because he says his character would want proximity to power. He is a professional actor named Nigel Pilkington (he played a dog walker on Slow Horses ) who is Christmas in Canterbury ’s antagonist, Alastair Sinclair. He says that when the camera starts rolling he is going to interact with me. Oh no . Someone down the choir stall—another professional actor, Emily Swain, playing the school headmistress—indicates that she’s going to look at me in a significant way when the song medley starts, because it includes the mayor’s favorite song. The mayor’s favorite song?! I feel like Jessy Schram as the amnesiac in Time for Them to Come Home for Christmas : I don’t know myself but keep discovering that I mean a lot to other people. Apparently the mayor is supposed to love this choral performance—information that I am learning right as the camera is about to roll. The mayor loves it so much that Jessy Schram gets to keep her job, despite all of the Vienna confusion. “Our Lord Mayor was in attendance tonight and was delighted with your rendition of her favorite carol” is a line in this movie— a fact I learn in real time as the actor says it, on camera, in front of me . It is fine. It’s fine! Acting is reacting. I can react. I live to react. All I have to do is make faces. Normal faces. Like Fiorello La Guardia. One of the ADs now explains what we are meant to do during this choral performance: enjoy it. My acting coach was right! First, we will clap politely for the other, lesser choir that is leaving the stage, and then we will go wild for the collaboration between Jessy’s and Will’s choirs. I can do this. Clack goes the clapper board. We are rolling. The lesser choir leaves. The boy choir members take their places onstage. The prerecorded vocal track of their singing starts to play, announced by a metronomic click - click - click . “ Gaudete, gaudete, Christus est natus .” The choir lip-synchs perfectly. Now the second choir—with girls!—runs onstage to join them. Jessy Schram gets pulled into the mix. To encourage the choir, the movie’s choreographer (Will Kemp’s sister) is gesturing exuberantly off camera. On camera, Jessy Schram is conducting! Will Kemp is also conducting! The choir is singing together . The camera pans over our row to see how we are taking this. This is the moment. My moment. I have no idea what faces I am making. I feel delirious. Whenever they yell “Cut,” I assume it’s because my face is ruining the sequence. I keep forgetting to look at Nigel. “I am making the weirdest faces I’ve ever made in my life,” I type into my Notes app. Fortunately, gaping open-mouthed like Fiorello La Guardia is actually correct for this mayor, who is supposed to be delighted by this children’s-choir performance. Oneida Crawford, the producer, drops by and compliments me on my reactions. She later suggests that I become a professional supporting artist. They … want more of me? I keep getting promoted. We are now going to film some cutaways to the mayor in conversation with Alastair and a character named Hans Mueller, who has arrived from Vienna, Austria , to reveal that Jessy Schram did not. He’s played by Will Kemp’s younger brother, Roland, a Pilates instructor who urges us to do “thoracic breaths” between takes. We move to a different choir stall. “You’re the Lord Mayor?” one of the children from the choir asks when we’re not rolling. “You’ve been to my house! You’re friends with my mom!” I have? I am? I seem to have completely crossed over to the Hallmark dimension. The next scene is as follows: Hans Mueller, the Lord Mayor, and Alastair are deep in conversation. A repentant Alastair needs to look up and bow in acknowledgment to Jessy Schram, and then he needs to get back to our conversation. Talking without talking is much harder than those other extras made it look. Here is a sample of our inaudible, improvised dialogue, as far as I can remember: HANS: Have you been to the beach? THE LORD MAYOR: I don’t know what you’re saying! I’m the mayor! HANS: I’ve been to the beach. THE LORD MAYOR: I am too busy to go to the beach, because I’m the mayor. This is apparently going so well that they decide to get a close-up of us talking. And they bring the microphone over. A microphone? Are they going to record us talking out loud? The camera starts rolling. Some moments feel as though they last much longer than they actually do. I imagine Thomas Becket thought that getting stabbed by those knights took a long time. “This cathedral certainly has a rich history,” Alastair improvises confidently, and I freeze. In this moment I am thinking many things. One is: How did I get here? Another: Do I attempt to do a British accent in conversation with actual British people, one of whom is a professional actor? I remember opening my mouth. I know that some form of sound must have come out of it. I have no recollection of what this sound was, other than that it did not come out in anything remotely like a British accent, whatever my intentions were. I think I may have said, “Indubitably”? I hear voices. “Show them your chain!” Is that the director herself, Shamim Sarif? Obediently, I brandish the chain. I can see the safety pin holding it in place. Temu Mayor , I think. “We spent all our budget on choirs,” I say out loud, in what is very clearly not a British accent. This is when I break. The forbidden laugh comes lurching out of me, in great sobs. Tears are pouring down my cheeks. My sweat is redolent of cinnamon. Somehow we are still rolling. “Does it have magical powers?” either Hans or Alastair is saying. I am fully hysterical. “It is a talisman,” I mutter, through my tears. I try to rescue the moment, as I did at the wedding, by saying, “I just loved the music so much.” This does not work. “We’ve lost the Lord Mayor,” someone says. The next day, I am talking with Jessy Schram. “I didn’t realize that the Lord Mayor was, like, the pivot point,” I tell her. We are standing outside Canterbury Cathedral in the final hours of filming. “Oh, you are actually a plot point,” she says. The mayor’s love of the choir performance is the only reason her character is allowed a job now in Canterbury. Jessy notes that, earlier in the script, her character references the existence of the Lord Mayor, saying that the song they’re set to perform (“Once in Royal David’s City”) is his favorite song. Then one of the choir girls corrects her. Not his . The Lord Mayor is a she . “So then when I turned around,” Jessy says, “and I saw you dressed in your beautiful jewel, I was so excited.” She felt that my mayor had a “really good vibe about her.” Is this more great acting from Jessy Schram, or did my acting coach work her own magic? Sophie Green for The Atlantic The children’s choir, another Hallmark ingredient, rehearses for the climactic sequence in the cathedral. Will Kemp also offers encouragement after I apologize for my giggle fit. “Sometimes you become so aware of the ridiculousness of what you’re really doing,” he says, “and you have a bit of an out-of-body experience. And then you either giggle, cry, or have to sit down, or you do all three. So you’re not alone.” A tear dribbles down my cheek. “You’re crying,” my Hallmark gentleman says. Are we having a moment? One of those moments that Joany Kane writes around? In fact, no. There is sunscreen in my eye. I think about fake things and real things and how Hallmark twists the two into a delicious candy cane. I think about how Joany Kane owes the love of her life to The Christmas Card . She was 34, two years before the Hallmark Channel even existed, working at a lumber mill and writing her screenplay for a Christmas romance. One day, when the loggers came to collect their pay, she locked eyes with one of them. It was a thunderbolt. It was the kind of thing that would happen in a Hallmark movie. And suddenly, not only had she found a love interest in Logger Honey (as she would call him) but also she had realized that her movie needed to be set at a lumber mill. True story and Hallmark story, real and fake, forever blended. When she finished the screenplay, she went to deliver a copy to Logger Honey for him to read and ended up back at his place. He played his favorite music. They danced. She spent the night. “Probably spending the first night together was not Hallmark,” Joany notes. “More like Netflix. Or, you know, Cinemax, 15 years ago. But it was true love for both of us.” She never left. It’s been 27 years. Maybe it’s possible to bridge the real and the fake. If it weren’t for Joany’s own life, The Christmas Card wouldn’t exist. If it weren’t for The Christmas Card , she wouldn’t have gone over to deliver the script to Logger Honey—and she wouldn’t now be waking up every day next to the love of her life. “Everybody’s chasing that moment of feeling,” Joany says. And if you can’t quite find that moment in real life, Hallmark has you covered. Now it’s time to catch that moment on film: the final kiss, in front of the cathedral. Our leads approach each other in their perfect coats. Snowboy’s machine blasts its foam into the sky. When the foam falls, it is snowing, even though I know it isn’t really. This winter in July is a kind of Christmas gift—something we are making, together, so that the world will be a little nicer. So that we can turn on the TV and see magic. Made magic. Which is, of course, the only kind we get. Night falls on Canterbury. As we get set up for the final shot, I watch the monitors. The crew sits against a wall, watching the monitors too. Will’s luminous, moisturized face is framed by two Christmas trees. For a moment, we are all watching a Hallmark movie. Nowhere on Earth is the artificiality more obvious than here, on the set, with the boom mic just off camera and the Snowboy machine going VOOOOOOOOOOOOM . Yet there, on the screen, it is briefly real. Magic. The ordinary, given back to us, properly illuminated. Christmas feels so close and tangible that I can almost smell it—a real pumpkin pie, baking very close by. Wait, never mind. That is my armpit. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “How I Became the Star* of a Hallmark Christmas Movie.”

items.title: Reading Isn’t Over Yet
items.description: The Age of Reading Is Over In the August issue, Rose Horowitch considered whether civilization can survive our postliterate era . Rose Horowitch’s “The Age of Reading Is Over” is devastating. The comparison between our present moment and the long, undramatic decline of the Library of Alexandria is apt: We are witnessing a gradual failure of will and attention. I am a conductor, and I was struck by the parallel with musical literacy. A score, like a serious book, demands an ability to hold a complex structure in your mind and resist the urge to skim. When that capacity atrophies, music becomes background, atmosphere, content. The difference between reading Doctor Zhivago and reading a romantasy novel is not unlike the difference between listening to a late Beethoven quartet and letting a playlist wash over you. David Woodard Tampere, Finland While I appreciate Rose Horowitch’s deep dive into the decline of literacy, I take issue with conflating concern about reading in general with concern about the specific kinds of literature people are reading. Though well-meaning, the story was full of judgmental rhetoric about graphic novels, audiobooks, and works of fiction with shorter and simpler sentences. One series I love, “The Empyrean,” was among those ridiculed in the article. Years ago, I absorbed such judgments subconsciously, and it caused me to take a decade-long break from reading. I started reading for pleasure again only when I gave myself permission to ignore what I thought I “should” read. I’m a Millennial mom of three kids, ages 10, 7, and 3. I take them to the library weekly and read to them every day. Raising them, I’ve learned to resist the urge to judge books as the “right kind” or “wrong kind.” Regardless of what they’re reading, my kids are using their imaginations, learning new concepts, exploring new perspectives, and strengthening their attention spans. Most important, they’re learning to follow their innate curiosity, laying the groundwork for a lifelong love of reading. Faigy Gilder Fair Lawn, N.J. One detail in Rose Horowitch’s article made me chuckle. Harvard’s assistant director for humanities and social-sciences support tells her about a student who “was struggling to read a book written in Old English”: Anthony Burgess’s 1962 novel A Clockwork Orange . That novel, however, is narrated in an invented futuristic slang that draws on Russian words. A sentence on page 1 begins: “Our pockets were full of deng, so there was no real need from the point of view of crasting any more pretty polly to tolchock some old veck in an alley.” It’s worrisome that Harvard students now find books hard to read, but, in their defense, some books actually are. Lawrence Levi Brooklyn, N.Y. Rose Horowitch’s assessment of the decline of reading reminded me of a passage in “The Prelude,” by William Wordsworth. In it, the narrator dreams of a Bedouin frantically riding across the desert on his dromedary ahead of a rising deluge that will drown the world. He carries a stone and a shell—the stone represents knowledge (symbolizing Euclid’s Elements ), and the shell, imagination. The rider searches for a place to bury them so they are not lost forever in the flood. It feels like a perfect analogue for our moment. Those of us who understand the importance of the long sentence are clutching our books and pens as we race ahead of what can seem like a drowning of critical thinking and the academy itself. I am not optimistic that we will find a safe place to hide them all before generative AI washes across the sands. Art Casale Kernersville, N.C. Rose Horowitch’s “The Age of Reading Is Over” is a fascinating and disturbing account of the decline of sustained reading. But I wonder whether “postliterate” is the right description of where humanity is going. The philosopher Ernst Cassirer called us animal symbolicum —the symbol-using animal. Long before widespread literacy, human beings communicated complex ideas through speech, gestures, pictures, music, numbers, and other symbols. Alphabetic writing was an extraordinary development in that history, but need not be our final form of communication. Horowitch rightly distinguishes reading words from the higher-order abilities of comprehension and synthesis. But must those abilities always depend on long-form prose? A composer can communicate through musical notation. A mathematician can compress an elaborate argument into a handful of symbols. And we communicate more and more through combinations of words, diagrams, photographs, and videos. I recently gave a group of Japanese business executives a 5,000-word English-language article for discussion. Rather than spend our meeting reading it, I used AI to reduce its argument to 16 slides. We absorbed the argument in about 15 minutes and spent the remaining time doing something distinctly human: questioning it and debating one another. Perhaps, then, we are witnessing not the death of literacy but another stage in the evolution of symbolic communication. The question is whether Homo literatus can give way to Homo symbolicum without losing the habits of thought that reading taught us. Dan Considine Tokyo, Japan The love of reading, even the necessity of reading, was a gift from my mother. She was a child of Depression-era deep poverty in East Texas, and for lack of clothes, adequate food, and family support, her education ended after eighth grade, despite her having been the spelling-bee champ that year. Yet somehow, she kept her love of reading alive. Years later, she was a stay-at-home mom raising three daughters on my father’s wages as a heavy-equipment operator—enough for food, basic clothing, and a roof over our heads, but not much more. Still, every few weeks, she would scrape together the taxi fare to take us to the library in downtown Garland, Texas. For me, that library was a secret door to another world. I was still in elementary school, but wandered the history section, reading about World War II and the Holocaust, and struggling through the novels of Thomas Hardy. Heady stuff. At home, we had few books, but we did have a blue-bound set of the Britannica Junior Encyclopedia . My mother had bought it from a door-to-door salesman on a monthly payment plan, with little prospect that the payments would ever be made. I kept those books through moves from Texas to Michigan, back to Texas, and finally to California. Barbara Jean Calfee Larkspur, Calif. My name is Aviya, and I am 9 years old. My grandparents subscribe to The Atlantic , and just a few minutes ago, I finished “The Age of Reading Is Over.” It was so interesting, but it also made me angry that there is a need to write about this topic! I wanted to let you know: There is still hope. My friends and I are avid readers and writers. Not to speak too soon, but my teachers still encourage us to read whole books. I have read many classic works of literature, such as the Little House series, by Laura Ingalls Wilder, and Anne of Green Gables , by Lucy Maud Montgomery, and I plan to start The Hobbit , by J. R. R. Tolkien, very soon. I am not getting my own cellphone until eighth grade. I love to write and draw, and many people I know do too. And I don’t know about you, but I’m pretty sure I still have plenty of white matter in my brain! Aviya Perlman Cresskill, N.J. Rose Horowitch replies: I’m aware of the irony of publishing almost 9,000 words about how little we read, so I’m grateful to everyone who took the time to get through the story and reflect on it. Many of your letters point to a tension that runs through the article. The arrival of our postliterate age is not due to any one person’s actions. I, too, often read short, simple works; listen to podcasts; and go days without opening a book. The broader cultural shift we’re seeing has emerged from millions of us making these same choices, day in and day out. Yet the stories shared by Aviya Perlman and Barbara Jean Calfee show the enduring effects of an individual’s love of reading and learning—and how that commitment can lead to a powerful resurgence of the practice in others. Behind the Cover In this month’s cover story, “ The Geo-Located Generation ,” Sarah Zhang explores how technologies that allow parents to track their children’s whereabouts have changed parenthood and childhood alike. These tools promise to assuage parents’ fears, Zhang writes, but they often generate new anxieties—and curtail the independence that young people once took for granted. For our cover image, the illustrator Miguel Porlan took a familiar image of parental care, a swan looking after a brood of cygnets, and gave it a modern twist. —Liz Hart , Art Director Correction “ The Babies Left Behind in America ” (November) misstated the name of Eber’s caregiver. Her name is Estela Díaz, not Estela Garcia. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “The Commons.”

items.title: Pakistan tighten grip on first Test as Sri Lanka struggle at 114-3
items.description: Pakistan strengthened their hold on the opening Test against Sri Lanka on Tuesday, declaring their first innings at 434 for nine before reducing the visitors to 114 for three at the close of the second day at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium. Sri Lanka, who still trail by 320 runs, will resume their innings on the third day with Kamindu Mendis unbeaten on 40 and captain Dhananjaya de Silva on 22. Their resistance came after Pakistan’s pace attack made early inroads, although bad light brought an end to play after 27.1 overs. Resuming at 281 for five, Pakistan built on their overnight position through a series of valuable contributions, with Saud Shakeel and debutant Ghazi Ghori adding 96 runs for the sixth wicket. Saud, who had reached 57 on the opening day, continued to anchor the innings but narrowly missed out on a century, falling for 93 off 199 balls after being caught behind off Asitha Fernando. Ghazi provided useful support with 48 before his dismissal brought debutant Arafat Minhas to the crease. Minhas made an impressive contribution, striking 52 off 72 deliveries, including nine boundaries and a six, to further strengthen Pakistan’s position. He was eventually dismissed by Dilshan Madushanka, while Razaullah added a brisk 10 before Pakistan declared in the 107th over. The innings was notable for the number of half-centuries, with five Pakistan batters reaching the milestone. Three of those came from debutants, as Tayyab Arif scored 57, Mohammad Taha made 51 and Minhas contributed 52. Captain Babar Azam also registered a half-century, while Shakeel’s 93 proved the highest individual score. Fernando and Madushanka shared six wickets between them, claiming three apiece, but Sri Lanka struggled to contain Pakistan’s batting depth. In reply, Pakistan’s fast bowlers quickly put the visitors under pressure. Mohammad Abbas provided the breakthrough by removing opener Pasindu Sooriyabandara for a duck, caught behind, before debutant Saqib Khan struck to dismiss Dinesh Chandimal for just one. Lahiru Udara attempted to stabilise the innings with a fighting 42, but Saqib struck again, having him caught behind by Ghazi to leave Sri Lanka in further trouble. With three wickets down, Mendis and de Silva showed greater composure, putting together an unbeaten 49-run partnership to prevent further setbacks. Mendis looked particularly assured, reaching 40, while de Silva remained not out on 22 as the pair negotiated Pakistan’s attack. However, the fading light prevented Pakistan from making further inroads, forcing the umpires to call an early close. Pakistan will resume on the third day firmly in control, with a substantial first-innings lead and three Sri Lankan wickets already in hand. The visitors, meanwhile, face the difficult task of rebuilding their innings and narrowing the deficit, with Mendis and de Silva carrying the responsibility of providing the resistance needed to keep them in the contest.

items.title: Dialogue social : le syndicalisme guinéen et le ministère du Travail scellent un pacte d’action à Kaloum
items.description: La Bourse du travail à Kaloum a servi de cadre, ce mardi 10 novembre 2026, à une rencontre stratégique à haute portée politique et sociale entre les représentants du Mouvement Syndical Guinéen (MSG) et la ministre de l’Emploi, du Travail et de la Protection Sociale, Ramatoulaye Camara. Dans un climat marqué à la fois par une exigence ferme de résultats et par une volonté partagée de concertation, les débats se sont articulés autour de l’urgence de garantir un travail décent, d'étendre la protection sociale et d'associer directement le monde du travail aux retombées du vaste programme industriel Simandou 2040. Prenant la parole au nom des centrales syndicales, Sophie Kourouma, Secrétaire Générale adjointe de la Confédération Nationale des Travailleurs de Guinée (CNTG), a rappelé d’emblée la responsabilité immense incombant au département ministériel, dont l'action touche directement le quotidien de l'ensemble de la population. Soulignant que la jeunesse constitue la première richesse de la nation, la responsable syndicale a qualifié l’insertion professionnelle des jeunes et des femmes de première urgence sociale. Elle a insisté sur l'exigence d'un travail décent par le respect rigoureux du Code du travail, la mise en œuvre effective des conventions collectives, le renforcement des normes de sécurité sur les chantiers et la lutte active contre la précarité. Mettant en avant l'importance d'étendre la couverture sociale aux acteurs de l'économie informelle, elle a réaffirmé que la paix sociale durable ne peut se construire que dans le dialogue permanent et constructif, loin des postures d’affrontement. Le cœur du plaidoyer syndical s'est ensuite focalisé sur le déploiement du programme Simandou 2040, qualifié de levier de transformation économique et de projet d'intégration minologique et industrielle majeur. La Secrétaire Générale adjointe a signifié la volonté ferme du mouvement syndical d'occuper toute sa place dans la gouvernance sociale de ce chantier historique, depuis la phase d'extraction minière jusqu'aux installations portuaires et au réseau d'entreprises sous-traitantes. Exigeant un droit de regard structuré sur l'application du droit du travail, le respect de la santé au travail et la priorité absolue accordée à l’emploi local, l'organisation syndicale entend agir en partenaire vigilant mais loyal, apportant son expertise du terrain et contribuant à la formation de la main-d'œuvre locale. Forte de son expérience passée au cœur des négociations nationales depuis 2022, la ministre a affirmé son attachement viscéral au dialogue social, qu'elle entend ériger en méthode de travail systématique et permanente sous l'autorité du Premier ministre. S'adressant aux responsables des différentes centrales, elle a lancé un appel vibrant à la cohésion et à l'unité d'action dans le respect de l'indépendance de chaque structure, préconisant un échange direct et préventif pour écarter tout risque de malentendu. Dans cette optique de refondation des relations professionnelles, le chef du département du Travail s'est engagé sur trois principes fondamentaux : la régularité des rencontres hors des périodes de crise, la sincérité dans le traitement des contraintes matérielles ou juridiques, et la rigueur dans le suivi opérationnel des engagements actés. La ministre a également annoncé l'organisation prochaine du processus de représentativité syndicale, visant à garantir des élections libres, transparentes et équitables, afin que la légitimité des représentants des travailleurs soit incontestable autour de la table des négociations. Répondant explicitement au plaidoyer formulé pour Simandou 2040, elle a confirmé l'engagement de son ministère à accompagner toutes les démarches visant à intégrer pleinement les partenaires sociaux au suivi des conditions de travail au sein du programme national. Pour clore son discours, Ramatoulaye Camara a détaillé cinq chantiers prioritaires pour son mandat : l'adéquation formation-emploi pour les jeunes diplômés, l'extension graduelle de la protection sociale aux travailleurs informels et ruraux, le renforcement de l'inspection du travail pour faire respecter la législation — illustré récemment par la promulgation du décret sur les maladies professionnelles indemnisables —, la médiation préventive des conflits et la féminisation de la gouvernance syndicale. Réaffirmant sa totale disponibilité et assurant que sa porte resterait ouverte à toutes les centrales sans partialité, la ministre a ouvert la séance aux interventions de la salle, marquant le lancement effectif d'un chapitre de travail collaboratif destiné à concilier attractivité économique et justice sociale en Guinée.

items.title: Un peuple, une passion, un seul combat : la victoire des « Lions » ! (Par Abdoulaye Fofana Seck)
items.description: Chers Lions, Ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026, face au Soudan, le stade Léopold Sédar Senghor sera bien plus que le théâtre d'une rencontre de football. Il sera le lieu d'un nouveau rendez-vous entre une équipe, son histoire et tout un peuple uni par une même passion. À l'occasion de cette rencontre comptant pour les éliminatoires de la Coupe d'Afrique des Nations 2027, je voudrais vous transmettre, avec une profonde conviction, les encouragements et le soutien total du Président de la Fédération Sénégalaise de Football, Monsieur Abdoulaye Fall, ainsi que ceux de toute la famille du football sénégalais. Chers Lions, vous n'êtes jamais seuls ! Derrière chacun de vos pas, derrière chaque ballon disputé, derrière chaque effort consenti, il y a les espoirs, les prières et les encouragements de millions de Sénégalaises et de Sénégalais. Il y a ces enfants qui portent fièrement votre maillot et rêvent de suivre vos traces. Il y a ces anciens qui ont ouvert la voie et construit, génération après génération, la grandeur de notre football. Il y a cette jeunesse qui voit en vous des modèles de courage, de discipline, de dépassement de soi et de réussite. Et il y a surtout ce peuple extraordinaire qui sait faire du football un langage universel, capable d'effacer les différences, de transcender les clivages et de rassembler toutes les sensibilités autour d'un même drapeau. Ce drapeau vert, jaune et rouge, frappé de son étoile verte, est votre plus belle responsabilité et votre plus grande source d'inspiration. Vous êtes les héritiers d'une histoire glorieuse. Vous êtes les dignes représentants d'une Nation qui a appris à croire en ses champions et qui nourrit désormais les plus grandes ambitions. Aujourd'hui, une nouvelle page s'ouvre avec Patrick Vieira à la tête de l'encadrement technique. Cette première rencontre à Dakar sous sa conduite doit être celle de l'enthousiasme retrouvé, de la confiance partagée et d'une ambition collective renouvelée. Nous savons votre talent. Nous connaissons votre potentiel. Nous croyons en votre capacité à relever les défis les plus exigeants. Mais nous savons aussi que les plus belles victoires ne se construisent pas seulement avec les pieds. Elles se gagnent avec le cœur, avec la tête, avec l'esprit de sacrifice et cette volonté farouche de ne jamais renoncer. Alors, chers Lions, entrez sur cette pelouse avec détermination. Soyez solidaires dans l'effort, généreux dans l'engagement et intraitables dans votre volonté de défendre nos couleurs. Que chaque minute de cette rencontre soit l'expression de votre fierté de représenter le Sénégal. Et à vous, merveilleux supporters sénégalais, nous lançons également un appel : Faisons du stade Léopold Sédar Senghor un immense écrin de ferveur, de fraternité et de communion patriotique. Laissons de côté les polémiques et les querelles stériles. Ce qui nous rassemble est infiniment plus grand que ce qui peut nous diviser. Quand les Lions entrent sur le terrain, il n'y a plus de différences, plus de chapelles, plus de camps. Il n'y a qu'un seul peuple, une seule passion et une seule ambition : voir triompher le Sénégal. Chers Lions, le peuple sénégalais vous fait confiance. À vous de transformer cette confiance en énergie, cette énergie en performance et cette performance en victoire. Que cette rencontre soit le point de départ d'une nouvelle dynamique, porteuse de succès, d'espérance et de fierté nationale. Que Dieu vous accompagne, vous protège et vous accorde la victoire ! CA KAW, CA KANAM, GAINDÉ YI ! UN PEUPLE – UN BUT – UNE FOI ! VIVE LES LIONS ! VIVE LE SÉNÉGAL ! Abdoulaye Fofana Seck Conseiller en communication / Porte-parole du Président de la Fédération Sénégalaise de Football

items.title: Gombe records 98 road crash deaths, 1,345 injuries in nine months — FRSC
items.description: By Ben Ngwakwe GOMBE — The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has disclosed that 98 persons were killed while 1,345 others sustained injuries in road traffic crashes recorded across Gombe State between January and September 2026. The FRSC Sector Commander in the state, Commander Samson Kaura, disclosed this on Tuesday in Gombe while addressing members of the Gombe State Council of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) during the commemoration of the 2026 World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims. Kaura said the command recorded 1,345 road traffic incidents during the nine-month period, adding that fatalities increased by six per cent compared with the corresponding period. He identified excessive speeding and reckless driving as major causes of road crashes and fatalities, warning that irresponsible road use continued to pose a serious threat to motorists and other road users. According to him, the annual World Day of Remembrance provides an opportunity to honour those who have lost their lives or sustained serious injuries in road crashes, while drawing attention to the need for stronger legal responses to traffic offences resulting in deaths and injuries. He said the commemoration also seeks to promote better support for crash victims and their families, as well as evidence-based interventions to prevent and ultimately eliminate road traffic deaths and injuries. The sector commander expressed concern that the fatalities recorded in the first nine months of 2026 had surpassed the figure for the whole of 2025. He said the command recorded 1,614 road traffic incidents in 2025, resulting in 92 deaths and 926 injuries. Kaura described the 2026 World Day of Remembrance as a campaign aimed at translating remembrance into concrete action, stressing the need for collective responsibility in addressing road traffic crashes. In his response, the Vice Chairman of the Gombe State NUJ Council, Emmanuel Akila, who represented the state chairman, Faruk Muazu Gombe, pledged the union’s continued cooperation with the FRSC in promoting road safety and development. Akila, however, urged the FRSC to strengthen collaboration with the union to identify and curb the activities of fake journalists in the state. He called on the corps to insist on proper identification of journalists during official engagements and other road-related activities to prevent impersonation and protect the integrity of the journalism profession. The NUJ vice chairman also urged the FRSC to intensify enforcement against vehicle overloading, describing the practice as one of the factors contributing to fatalities in road crashes. He stressed the need for sustained public enlightenment, effective enforcement of traffic regulations and stronger collaboration among relevant stakeholders to reduce road crashes and safeguard lives on the highways. The post Gombe records 98 road crash deaths, 1,345 injuries in nine months — FRSC appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Lahore’s PM2.5 level eight times WHO guideline, report says
items.description: LAHORE: Satellite data detected 16,714 likely crop-residue fires in Punjab between Oct 1 and Nov 9, while Lahore’s average PM2.5 concentration was eight times the World Health Organisation’s (WHO) guideline value, according to a report by the Pakistan Air Quality Initiative (PAQI) that questioned the link between Diwali fireworks in India and the city’s pollution. The report, released on Tuesday, said the number of likely crop-residue fires in Punjab, Pakistan, remained almost unchanged from the corresponding period last year. Lahore’s average PM2.5 concentration stood at 126 micrograms per cubic metre during the period, exceeding the 24-hour National Environmental Quality Standards (NEQS) on all 40 days for which valid data were available. The average was 11pc lower than in the corresponding period in 2025. Satellite instruments detected 18,825 fires across Punjab, Pakistan, 89 per cent of which were classified as likely crop-residue burning. The highest daily count was recorded on Nov 1, with 1,102 detections. The 24-hour National Environmental Quality Standards (NEQS) were exceeded on all 40 days for which valid data were available. The average concentration was 11pc lower than during the corresponding period in 2025. Sheikhupura recorded the highest number of fires at 2,559, followed by Jhang (2,192), Okara (2,062), Hafizabad (1,893) and Gujranwala (1,417). The five districts accounted for 54pc of the total detections. The report found a positive correlation between upwind fire activity and PM2.5 levels in Lahore. On days when air trajectories passed over areas where burning was taking place, the average concentration reached 175 micrograms per cubic metre, compared with 93 micrograms on other days. A similar pattern was observed in Multan, where average PM2.5 levels reached 203 micrograms on days influenced by fires, compared with 88 micrograms on other days. In Bahawalpur, the corresponding figures were 125 and 65 micrograms. However, the report cautioned that the association did not establish the precise contribution of crop-residue burning to urban pollution, as stagnant weather conditions and reduced atmospheric dispersion also contributed to the accumulation of pollutants. The number of likely crop-residue fires in Punjab, Pakistan, was 8pc above the 2020-2025 average, although the comparable satellite record showed a 1pc decline from 2025. The assessment also examined whether fireworks during Diwali celebrations in India on Nov 8 had contributed to deteriorating air quality in Punjab. It found that easterly winds carried air from Indian territory towards Pakistan during the night. Of the 48 back trajectories arriving in Lahore, Kasur and Sialkot between 9pm on Nov 8 and midnight on Nov 10, 45 had passed over Indian territory within the preceding 12 hours, most frequently near Tarn Taran, Amritsar and Jammu. However, the report said the available evidence did not support attributing Lahore’s poor air quality after Diwali to fireworks across the border. Lahore’s average PM2.5 concentration between 6pm on Nov 8 and 1am on Nov 10 was 234 micrograms per cubic metre, 10pc higher than the average recorded during the same hours over the preceding seven days. In comparison, the average concentration in Kasur increased by 27pc and in Sialkot by 33pc, while Narowal recorded a 2pc decline. The increase was greater in cities farther from the international border. Faisalabad, located 130 kilometres from the border, recorded a 40pc increase, while Multan, 180km away, also saw a 40pc rise. The average increase in the four border cities — Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot and Narowal — was 36 micrograms per cubic metre, compared with 85 micrograms in Faisalabad and Multan. The report noted that pollution transported from across the border would be expected to cause a greater increase in border areas than in cities farther inland. However, the observed pattern did not support that explanation. Sialkot was an exception, recording a 37pc increase in PM2.5 during the night after Diwali, with air trajectories passing over the Jammu area. The assessment also found that emissions from New Delhi had not reached Lahore during the period analysed. Air from Delhi entered Pakistan near Rahim Yar Khan and Bahawalpur only after 3am on Nov 10, with its closest approach to Lahore remaining 266 kilometres away. The report said distinguishing between emissions from fireworks and smoke from agricultural fires required chemical analysis of particulate matter, including elements such as potassium, strontium and barium, which Pakistani monitoring stations did not measure. Air quality improves Meanwhile, the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department (EPCCD) reported an improvement in Lahore’s air quality on Monday following emergency mitigation and enforcement operations. The city’s average air quality index (AQI) reading, recorded at 489 at 9am, fell to 232 by 3pm — a reduction of 257 points, or approximately 53pc — according to the department’s monitoring network. Data from all 11 monitoring stations showed a decline in AQI readings during the period. Egerton Road recorded the biggest improvement, with its reading falling from 500 to 167, followed by GT Road, where the AQI dropped from 500 to 172. DHA Phase 6, Shahdara, Barki Road and Punjab University also recorded improvements, as did Wagah Border, Gulberg III, Kahna Nau, Safari Park and Multan Road. The department said multiple anti-smog guns had been deployed along high-traffic corridors and at dust-prone locations and pollution hotspots, while mist-sprinkling operations covered around 640 kilometres of designated routes. The government had earlier warned of deteriorating air quality in Lahore, Kasur and adjoining border districts on Nov 9 and 10, identifying Diwali fireworks, agricultural residue burning in Indian Punjab, easterly winds and stagnant atmospheric conditions as potential contributing factors. A special assessment issued on Nov 8 had cited 2,347 incidents of crop- residue burning in Indian Punjab up to Nov 4. Of these, 1,081 were recorded in the districts of Tarn Taran, Ferozepur and Amritsar. It had also warned that smoke from Diwali fireworks could reach Lahore within five to 13 hours, depending on wind conditions. EPCCD Secretary Silwat Saeed said the department was responding to deteriorating air quality through coordinated enforcement, real-time environmental monitoring and targeted field interventions. She said the department was using its monitoring infrastructure and Punjab Climate Watch data to identify pollution hotspots and direct operational teams to areas requiring immediate action. Environment Protection Agency (EPA) Director General Abdullah Nayyar Sheikh said the department had adopted a zero-tolerance approach towards major sources of air pollution. He said Quick Response Units were responding to satellite-detected fire anomalies and reports of crop-residue burning, with field teams being dispatched to extinguish fires and take action against those responsible. He added that inspections of factories, brick kilns and other emission-generating units had been intensified, while anti-smog gun operations were being carried out at full capacity in Lahore. The director general said the improvement recorded at all 11 monitoring stations was encouraging, but enforcement, surveillance and mitigation operations would continue. The PAQI report indicated a very high number of fires in areas upwind of Lahore on Nov 10, 11 and 12, with 642, 668 and 617 fires, respectively, expected under forecast wind conditions. Rain forecast Separately, the Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) on Tuesday forecast rain in most districts of Punjab over the next two days, saying it was likely to reduce smog but intensify cold weather. According to a PDMA alert issued on Tuesday, Lahore, Kasur, Sialkot, Narowal, Gujrat, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Wazirabad and Sheikhupura are among the districts likely to receive rainfall. Rain has also been forecast in Rawalpindi, Mianwali, Jhelum, Mandi Bahauddin, Attock, Chakwal, Khushab, Bhakkar, Sargodha, Murree and adjoining areas. The authority also forecast strong winds, rain and isolated hailstorms in Dera Ghazi Khan, Layyah, Bhakkar, Multan and adjoining areas. The PDMA directed commissioners and deputy commissioners across the province to remain alert and advised citizens to avoid unnecessary travel during storms and seek shelter in safe places. It also warned people against staying in open areas during thunderstorms and lightning.

items.title: L’ouragan CAMARA Djenabou Touré en 100 jours d’exception au MATD
items.description: « En politique, si vous voulez des discours, demandez à un homme. Si vous voulez des actes, demandez à une femme. » Cette formule célèbre de Margaret Thatcher trouve une illustration concrète dans la conduite des affaires publiques en Guinée sous le leadership du président Mamadi DOUMBOUYA. À la tête du Ministère de l’Administration du Territoire et de la Décentralisation (MATD), Madame CAMARA Djenabou Touré vient de traverser tel un ouragan le pont en lianes hautement symbolique des cent jours d’exercice, avec la maîtrise de l’ingénierie traditionnelle et le passage réussi vers une nouvelle rive institutionnelle. Cent jours d’engagement ininterrompu, d’initiatives concrètes et de réformes structurantes qui incarnent avec force la vision d’une administration réinventée. Sous le leadership éclairé du président Mamadi DOUMBOUYA , et conformément aux orientations du Gouvernement dirigé par le Premier ministre, M. Amadou Oury Bah, la ministre Djenabou Touré a insufflé une dynamique décisive. Au regard des indicateurs de performance, son action s’articule autour de « principes clairs : la modernisation de l’appareil administratif, le renforcement de la gouvernance territoriale, l’affirmation de la solidarité nationale et la délivrance de services publics de proximité performants et accessibles à tous. » Cette première étape du magistère ministériel se traduit par un bilan chiffré particulièrement parlant. À date, 72 actions hautement prioritaires programmées lors de sa prise de fonction ont été réalisées (dont 63 intégralement finalisées), 6 connaissent une avancée significative et 3 demeurent inscrites à l’agenda opérationnel, concrétisant ainsi un taux de réalisation exceptionnel de 87,5 %. Cette performance reflète l’immense capacité de mobilisation des équipes du département et confirme l’instauration irrésistible d’une culture du résultat au service exclusif des citoyens guinéens. Excellence institutionnelle, proximité citoyenne Le choix porté par le président Mamadi DOUMBOUYA sur Madame CAMARA Djenabou Touré relève d’une évidence stratégique tant le profil de la républicaine tire sa force d’une dimension intellectuelle, technique et humaine hors du commun. Bien avant sa nomination à ce portefeuille névralgique, la patriote arpentait déjà les pistes et les préfectures de la Guinée profonde, portée par une connaissance intime, viscérale et transversale des réalités socio-anthropologiques de nos terroirs. Cette maîtrise absolue des enjeux locaux, alliée à une proximité humaine forgée sur le terrain, lui permet de conduire la gouvernance territoriale avec la précision et l’assurance d’une praticienne avertie du terrain. À cet ancrage territorial d’exception s’ajoute une carrure internationale qui fait la fierté de toute une nation. Sa maîtrise parfaite de la langue anglaise en fait une diplomate chevronnée et une citoyenne du monde sans barrière linguistique, capable de porter haut la voix de la Guinée et de négocier avec une aisance remarquable auprès des chancelleries et des grands acteurs multilatéraux. Surtout, la ministre Djenabou Touré jouit d’une réputation de référence mondiale absolue dans le domaine de l’ingénierie démocratique et électorale. Unanimement saluée par les plus hautes institutions internationales, son expertise électorale d’élite la place au sommet du continent africain et sur l’échiquier global parmi les esprits les plus brillants et les plus respectés de sa génération. À cela s’ajoute son expertise sur l’état civil et la gestion des collectivités décentralisées. Cette virtuosité s’est illustrée par une présence permanente sur tous les fronts de la gouvernance administrative et de la modernisation de l’État. Les décrets du 20 août 2026, portant érection de sous-préfectures en préfectures et de préfectures en régions administratives, constituent une avancée majeure pour rapprocher le pouvoir décisionnel des populations. Cette réorganisation physique s’est doublée, le 13 octobre 2026, de l’adoption d’arrêtés historiques fixant la classification des types de communes et leurs organigrammes. Pour veiller à l’application rigoureuse de ces orientations, la républicaine s’est rendue sur le terrain du 13 au 20 octobre 2026 dans les régions de Kankan et Siguiri, arpentant les localités de Sabadou Baranama, Tokounou, Kintinian, Siguirini, Doko et Dialakoro pour dialoguer directement avec les élus, les sages et les citoyens autour du respect du domaine public et de la cohésion sociale. En parallèle, le département a accéléré la modernisation de l’état civil à travers l’Office National de l’État Civil et de l’Identification (ONECI), le Registre National des Personnes Physiques (RNPP), le Registre National de l’État Civil (RENEC) et la plateforme d’interopérabilité Yama-Yigui aux côtés de NG Technologie et DIGITECH. Célébrée le 16 septembre 2026 à Tombolia lors de la Journée Internationale de l’Identité, cette vision garantit à chaque Guinéen une identité numérique fiable et sécurisée. Cette démarche s’est accompagnée d’une solidarité active face aux épreuves de la Nation, notamment lors des drames de Dar-es-Salam et Hafia avec l’appui de l’ANGUCH, assurant un hébergement temporaire, une allocation gouvernementale de réinstallation de 21 millions de francs guinéens par ménage et un hommage appuyé lors des obsèques collectives du 4 septembre 2026. Sur le plan sous-régional et international, la patriote a consolidé des partenariats stratégiques avec la Banque mondiale, l’UNICEF et la signature de conventions avec l’OIF, le PNUD etc , tout en échangeant avec la Sierra Leone sur la sécurité frontalière. Cette dynamique a stimulé le développement local avec la pose des premières pierres de marchés modernes à Fassia (Sanoyah), Matoto (ancien cinéma Mimo) et Matam-Centre, l’alignement avec la vision Simandou 2040, et l’assainissement de Conakry (actions directes à Nongo-Kiroty et Matam, visite de la ZTT de Batipor et concertation stratégique du 22 octobre 2026 avec les 13 maires, l’ANASP et l’ASCAD). La valorisation des ressources humaines a également progressé via le CNFPATEL, la formation des cadres politiques et le Team Building de Rio Pongo (Boffa) du 9 au 11 octobre 2026. Au terme de ces cent premiers jours, la ministre Djenabou Touré a démontré qu’une gestion fondée sur l’exigence, l’intégrité et la vision prospective transforme durablement l’action publique. Actuellement, Mme Camara Djenabou Touré prépare sereinement les grandes échéances républicaines, notamment l’organisation rigoureuse des prochaines élections régionales et sénatoriales et le dialogue permanent avec les administrateurs territoriaux engagé le 6 octobre 2026. Cent jours d’engagement. Cent jours d’action. Une même ambition, celle de bâtir une administration territoriale performante au service de la Guinée et des Guinéens. Et maintenant, en guise de conclusion, faisons une halte en France, patrie des Lumières, pour rappeler, dans un esprit inspiré de Simone de Beauvoir, que la ministre Mme Camara Djenabou Touré démontre que le véritable leadership ne réside pas dans la simple proclamation d’intentions, mais dans la concrétisation tangible de résultats qui façonnent l’avenir d’un peuple. De Londres à Paris, jusqu’à Conakry, la maxime selon laquelle « on ne naît pas accompli, on le devient par l’action et par les œuvres que l’on édifie pour autrui » résonne avec force et motive davantage le leadership féminin. Il s’agit là d’inscrire dans la durée des actes pérennes au bénéfice de la République. Investie de cette mission élevée, Mme Camara Djenabou Touré fait du respect des délais et de l’exigence d’excellence son unique boussole. Pour l’histoire, la ministre de la République poursuit ainsi son action tel un ouragan de bienfaisance, véritable élan salvateur tant attendu en ce début de la belle saison de la Cinquième République, pour sceller toujours plus de résultats au compte du gouvernement Amadou Oury Bah sous le leadership du président Mamadi DOUMBOUYA . Le tout au bénéfice du peuple de Guinée, debout et fier de l’être ! Ibrahima DIALLO , Journaliste et écrivain. Conakry – Guinée.

items.title: Vaccination animale : Démarrage d’une nouvelle campagne
items.description: © Internet Près de 89 millions de têtes sont visées en 2026-2027. Le lancement officiel aura lieu dans le cercle de Fana. La campagne précédente avait retenu un objectif de 83,427 millions d’animaux et de volailles. Celui annoncé vendredi atteint précisément 88 741 618 têtes, soit une progression d’environ 5,3 millions ou 6,4 %. La cérémonie de lancement est fixée au 12 décembre au marché à bétail de Zantiguila, dans la commune rurale de Marakacoungo. Le gouvernement présente l’opération comme un moyen d’améliorer la couverture vaccinale et la surveillance des maladies animales. Le communiqué n’indique pas encore la répartition des doses par région, par espèce ou par maladie. Il ne précise pas non plus le budget, le coût supporté par les éleveurs, le calendrier des équipes vétérinaires ni les quantités de vaccins déjà disponibles. Ces données sont particulièrement utiles dans les zones de transhumance, où les troupeaux se déplacent sur de longues distances. L’objectif national regroupe les animaux et la volaille. Sa formulation ne permet pas de savoir si chaque tête sera comptée une seule fois ou si plusieurs vaccinations appliquées au même animal pourront entrer dans le bilan. Cette précision compte pour comparer la cible annoncée avec les résultats futurs. Un précédent bilan publié par les services publics faisait état de 41 068 999 animaux vaccinés sur une prévision de 76 860 210 lors de la campagne 2024, soit un taux d’exécution de 53,43 %. Ce résultat appartient à un exercice antérieur et ne renseigne pas encore sur la campagne 2025-2026. Lors du lancement de décembre 2025, le ministère avait cité plusieurs maladies animales encore présentes dans le pays. Il avait également insisté sur le marquage des petits ruminants et sur l’identification numérique du bétail. Le communiqué de cette année ne précise pas si ces deux composantes seront reprises dans les mêmes conditions. Pour les familles vivant de l’élevage, la santé du troupeau agit directement sur la vente des animaux, la production de lait et les pertes liées aux épizooties. L’écart entre l’objectif national et les vaccinations réalisées donnera la mesure de la couverture réelle de la campagne.

items.title: L’Algérie, principal importateur de viandes d’Espagne en dehors de l’UE
items.description: L'Espagne s'impose comme le premier fournisseur de viandes rouges à l'Algérie. En 2025, plus de la moitié des importations algériennes de viandes rouges provenaient de l'Espagne . Dans sa fiche sectorielle consacrée au marché algérien de la viande rouge , publiée lundi 9 novembre 2026, l’Office Économique et Commercial d’Espagne à Alger dévoile que l'Espagne domine le marché algérien et devance largement ses concurrents. Viandes rouges en Algérie : plus de 300 millions d'euros importées d'Espagne en 2025 Cette fiche fait savoir que l'Algérie a importé pour 332 millions d'euros de viandes rouges d'Espagne durant l'année 2025. Il s'agit de la moitié des importations algériennes en viandes ovines et bovines réfrigérées. L'Espagne se positionne ainsi comme le premier fournisseur de l'Algérie de viandes fraîches. L'Espagne domine notamment la filière ovine, avec une part de marché atteignant les 98 %, indique la même source. Pour ce qui est de la filière bovine, l'Espagne a pu fournir 60 % de la valeur des importations algériennes au premier trimestre de 2026, s'imposant également comme le premier fournisseur du pays en la matière. L’Office Économique et Commercial d’Espagne à Alger précise que « l'Espagne occupe une position dominante » dans le secteur de la viande rouge en Algérie. Rappelant que la production locale est loin de répondre à la demande du marché, il conclut que les importations constituent une nécessité pour l'Algérie. L'Algérie, premier marché de viande bovine espagnole en 2026 De son côté, l'Algérie occupe une place importante pour l'Espagne, vu que le marché algérien a absorbé, entre janvier 2026 et mai 2026, 62 % des exportations espagnoles de viande bovine en dehors de l'Union européenne. Toujours selon la même source, l'Espagne a pu dominer le marché algérien des viandes rouges grâce à sa proximité géographique avec l'Algérie, mais aussi « à la qualité et à la réputation des produits espagnols » ainsi qu'à « la régularité de l'approvisionnement » et à « l'adaptation aux spécifications des acheteurs « . L'office économique et commercial d'Espagne à Alger rappelle enfin que l'importation des viandes rouges en Algérie est soumise à « un cadre réglementaire exigeant « , notamment au programme prévisionnel d'importation (PPI), aux autorisations vétérinaires délivrées par les instances sanitaires algériennes, mais aussi au certifications halal. L’article L'Algérie, principal importateur de viandes d'Espagne en dehors de l'UE est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Enseignants-chercheurs : la grève universitaire entre dans sa troisième semaine
items.description: © Internet Le Comité exécutif national du Syndicat national de l’enseignement supérieur et de la recherche scientifique (CEN-SNESUP) maintient son arrêt de travail pour une durée indéterminée. La prime de recherche reste son unique revendication annoncée. Une délégation du Haut Conseil islamique, du Réseau des communicateurs traditionnels du Mali et des chefs de quartier de la Commune II a rencontré les responsables syndicaux samedi 7 novembre. La réunion s’est tenue à la Faculté d’histoire et de géographie. La démarche visait à comprendre le fondement du mouvement lancé le 26 octobre. Les médiateurs ont fait part de leur disponibilité pour faciliter le dialogue, mais aucun accord ni calendrier de reprise n’a été annoncé après la rencontre. La grève touche au moins une dizaine d’établissements d’enseignement supérieur et de recherche. Le CEN-SNESUP affirme que le mouvement se poursuivra jusqu’à l’application de la prime, la fixation de son montant et le règlement des rappels qu’il réclame. Ces trois demandes se rattachent au même point de revendication. Le texte réglementaire invoqué par le syndicat existe. L’article 34 du décret d’application du statut des enseignants-chercheurs, publié en novembre 2017, inscrit la prime de recherche parmi les primes et indemnités accordées à cette catégorie de personnel. L’article 41 renvoie cependant la fixation des montants à un autre décret pris en Conseil des ministres. La présence de la prime dans le statut et son paiement effectif constituent ainsi deux étapes distinctes. Le syndicat estime que la seconde reste en attente depuis près de neuf ans. Aucune proposition chiffrée du gouvernement ni aucun calendrier d’application n’avaient été rendus publics lundi matin. Pour les étudiants, la prolongation du mouvement signifie de nouveaux cours suspendus et des programmes décalés. L’ampleur précise varie suivant les établissements et leurs calendriers. Les informations disponibles ne permettent pas d’annoncer une modification générale des dates d’examens ou de l’année universitaire. La rencontre de samedi ouvre une médiation extérieure aux discussions habituelles entre le ministère et le syndicat. Sa poursuite dépendra des contacts annoncés par les représentants religieux, traditionnels et communautaires.

items.title: Political narratives and allegations have a limited 'shelf life', CM Maryam says
items.description: JHELUM: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz on Tuesday said political narratives, allegations and criticism had a limited “shelf life”, asserting that public service and development work ultimately determined electoral success. She was speaking at a Honhaar Scholarship and laptop distribution ceremony at Government Comprehensive High School in Jhelum. During her address, Maryam said voters did not support political narratives but instead judged political parties by their public service record. She cited the PML-N’s victories in recent local elections in Sahiwal and Gujranwala, despite opposition parties having “joined hands” against her. “No matter how much you talk or how many claims you make, if you have not served the people, there comes a day when you are deprived [of public support],” she said. “If some people have objections and are levelling allegations of corruption against the Punjab government, why don’t they resign from the cabinet?” the provincial chief executive said, in an apparent reference to Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik’s recent allegations of corruption against the Punjab government. She maintained that there had been no corruption in the development projects worth trillions of rupees launched by her government over the past three years. Referring to the opposition’s criticism of her government, Maryam said attempts were being made to distract her as elections drew closer. She said she was answerable to the people for the expenditure of public money, adding that she would not spare any minister or official against whom evidence of corruption or bribery was presented. “I have not said that corruption has completely ended in Punjab,” she said. The chief minister said she would not comment on other provinces, as their respective governments were answerable to their own populations. However, she claimed that Punjab was the only province where the chief minister pursued a new corruption case every day. Maryam asserted that her government had broken the tradition of concentrating development spending in major cities. She cited the expansion of the Green Bus service to cities including Jhelum, Khushab, Layyah, Bhakkar, Rahim Yar Khan, Bahawalpur and Multan, saying similar transport facilities and infrastructure were being provided across the province. The chief minister also highlighted the establishment of Nawaz Sharif Schools of Eminence, saying they were comparable to expensive private schools. She said the schools offered facilities such as air-conditioned classrooms, computer laboratories, artificial intelligence laboratories and science laboratories, along with qualified faculty. Maryam also praised provincial Education Minister Rana Sikandar Hayat for his work in the education sector. She announced that 300 Nawaz Sharif Schools of Eminence would be established, with work on the initiative in Jhelum scheduled to begin on Dec 15. She further said the government was establishing cardiac treatment facilities in 25 cities where such services had previously been unavailable. Patients visiting catheterisation laboratories (cath labs) at public hospitals would be able to receive procedures, including angiograms, angioplasty, stenting and pacemaker implantation, free of cost, she added. She further said cancer hospitals were being established in every divisional headquarters, while the country’s first government-run cancer hospital was being built in Lahore. On Friday, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif claimed that Salik’s recent corruption allegations against the Punjab government are part of efforts to set the ground for an “alternative arrangement”. He alleged that Salik’s allegations “are part of setting the stage for some post-period”. “This statement was given selectively against Punjab. Corruption is prevalent everywhere in Pakistan. […] I have tweeted about it many times,” he added. Asif continued: “There is an attempt to create an alternative arrangement — to discredit incumbent people so that a fresh team can be presented. Whoever is behind this, that is what I was signalling to. Please do not ask me anything more than this; I can share my personal assessment.” What did Salik say? During a talk show on a private television channel last week, the Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) leader praised former Punjab chief minister and his uncle Chaudhry Pervez Elahi , further criticising the incumbent provincial administration headed by Chief Minister Maryam and alleging that he regularly heard complaints of corruption. He also questioned lavish government spending , particularly the use of an official aircraft , arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties. He said officials using government aircraft should be required to demonstrate the tangible outcomes and public benefits of their trips. He also called for greater ministerial accountability, proposing that federal and provincial ministers should be empowered to perform their duties while also being held accountable for their performance. Salik’s remarks carry particular political significance given the fractured relationship between the Chaudhry family and the PTI leadership. Salik, the younger son of PML-Q president Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, belongs to a family whose political loyalties have diverged sharply since the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in 2022 through a no-confidence vote. While Elahi and his son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, aligned themselves with the PTI, the Shujaat family chose to stand with the Sharifs. Salik’s elder brother, Shafay Hussain, is also part of CM Maryam’s cabinet in Punjab. Last Tuesday, CM Maryam said she had sent a Rs5 billion defamation notice to Salik, demanding that he retract his remarks. She claimed the PML-Q leader’s anger stemmed from neither corruption nor progress and the issue was that she had changed the deputy commissioner of Gujrat a few days earlier, whereas Salik wanted a DC of his choice to be appointed. Meanwhile, responding to Maryam’s remarks, Salik said he stood by his statement and had responded honestly to a question during the interview.
